Lesson 4: Intro

00:07.080 --> 00:14.360 These include the environment in which the AI agent interacts with sensors, allowing the agent to perceive 00:14.360 --> 00:15.360 its environment. 00:15.920 --> 00:21.680 The model, which helps the agent interpret its perceptions and guide its understanding.

Core Concept

In this section of the course, we'll explore the key components involved in building AI agents. These include the environment in which the AI agent interacts with sensors, allowing the agent to perceive its environment. The model, which helps the agent interpret its perceptions and guide its understanding.

Key Points

  • Decision making logic which determines how the agent selects appropriate actions and actuators.
  • The mechanisms through which the agent executes actions and affects its environment.
  • And lastly, the feedback mechanisms allow the agent to evaluate whether it has successfully achieved its intended goals.
  • These lessons are important because they give you a foundational understanding of the building blocks used to create AI agents in practice.

Lesson 5: Environment – The External World That the Agent Perceives and Interacts With

00:02.200 --> 00:10.160 As we've discussed, AI agents can handle a wide range of tasks and adapt to changing conditions in 00:10.160 --> 00:11.040 real time. 00:11.440 --> 00:14.720 This means they're able to work in a changing environment.

Core Concept

The environment is everything external to the agent. It defines the problem space, constraints,

and possibilities.

Key Points

The environment dictates sensors needed and actions possible.

Can be physical (roads, weather) or digital (websites, databases).

Agent design MUST align with its operational environment.

Agents must learn from environments like humans do.

Examples

Self-driving car

Roads, vehicles, pedestrians, weather. Complex, dynamic scenarios.

PE: Test Floor

Tester hardware, handlers, temperature chambers, production schedules. Must navigate

equipment limitations and yield targets.

Environment Properties

Fully vs. Partially observable - can the agent see everything?

Deterministic vs. Stochastic - are outcomes predictable?

Static vs. Dynamic - does it change during deliberation?

Discrete vs. Continuous - finite states or infinite?

Single vs. Multi-agent - alone or competing?

Key Takeaways

Define the environment FIRST.

Misalignment between agent and environment = failure.

💡 From the Lecture
00:11.440 --> 00:14.720 This means they're able to work in a changing environment.
💡 From the Lecture
01:53.770 --> 02:01.090 This means that in some cases, an AI agent's environment comprises both digital data such as product 02:01.090 --> 02:09.570 information, user preferences or browsing history, and real world factors like weather conditions, 02:09.610 --> 02:12.610 location, or even local events.

Lesson 6: Sensors – How the Agent Collects Data About its Surroundings

00:00.080 --> 00:05.280 We often overlook the remarkable capabilities of the human brain. 00:05.720 --> 00:11.080 They allow us to see the world around us and collect vast amounts of information. 00:11.640 --> 00:19.160 Our minds process countless details, subconsciously using our senses to absorb what we see, hear, 00:19.160 --> 00:19.960 and taste.

Core Concept

Mechanisms that allow agents to receive input from surroundings.

Types

Physical: cameras, lidar, GPS, IoT

Digital: web scrapers, APIs, database queries

Hybrid: physical sensors + internet connectivity

Examples

Self-driving car

Cameras + lidar + GPS + traffic APIs fused together.

PE: Test Data

STDF datalogs, SPC systems, equipment APIs, yield databases.

Key Takeaways

No sensors = blind agent.

Sensor fusion (multiple sources) gives richer understanding.

Sensor choice must match environment.

💡 From the Lecture
01:00.000 --> 01:07.550 Essentially, sensors enable AI agents to perceive their surroundings in much the same way human senses 01:07.550 --> 01:07.950 do.

Lesson 7: Model – the Agent’s Way of Making Sense of Information

00:00.160 --> 00:08.520 Now we know that agents receive abundant data through sensors, much like how our eyes and ears collect 00:08.520 --> 00:10.760 information from our surroundings. 00:11.400 --> 00:14.840 But collecting data is just the first step.

Core Concept

The agent's brain. Processes sensor data into meaningful understanding.

Spectrum

Simple ML: decision trees, regression - fast, interpretable

Neural Networks: pattern recognition - powerful, less interpretable

LLMs: human-like reasoning, multi-step planning - most capable

Additional Context

LLMs as central reasoning engine; tools handle execution. Model = WHAT to do; Tools = HOW.

Key Takeaways

More capable models = more capable agents (but more cost).

Multimodal models unify perception across data types.

Understanding without action is useless.

💡 From the Lecture
00:58.480 --> 01:06.440 These multimodal capabilities enhance context awareness, allowing AI agents to perform effectively 01:06.640 --> 01:10.920 in real world, complex and dynamic environments.

Lesson 8: Decision-making Logic – Rules and Objectives that Guide the Agent’s Actions

00:00.400 --> 00:05.920 So far, our agent has received information from the environment and analyzed it. 00:06.240 --> 00:10.600 The next step is to determine the most appropriate course of action. 00:10.920 --> 00:17.920 The agent needs a mechanism responsible for evaluating different options, allowing it to decide the 00:17.920 --> 00:19.360 best course of action.

Core Concept

Evaluates options and commits to action. Bridges understanding and execution.

Examples

Trading Agent

Only invest if return > 7% AND volatility < 15%.

PE: Disposition Logic

If delta < 3 sigma AND no spec exceedance, PASS.

Approaches

Rule-based: predictable, auditable

Probabilistic: handles uncertainty

LLM reasoning: flexible, less predictable

Hybrid: LLM proposes + logic layer validates (recommended)

Key Takeaways

For high-stakes domains, always add a validation layer.

LLM = employee proposing; Logic layer = manager approving.

💡 From the Lecture
00:52.040 --> 00:58.400 For example, the decision making logic layer could review the output from the model and admit only 00:58.400 --> 01:06.430 investments with expected return that is higher than 7% and volatility lower than 15%.
💡 From the Lecture
01:19.310 --> 01:21.550 Consider a spam filter agent.

Lesson 9: Actions – How the Agent Shapes the Environment

00:02.040 --> 00:07.800 We've reached the stage where the agent performs an action and influences the environment. 00:08.520 --> 00:11.200 A self-driving car drives down the road. 00:11.360 --> 00:14.280 A customer support agent sends chat messages.

Core Concept

What the agent DOES to influence its environment. Closes the loop between thinking and

impact.

The Feedback Loop

Act: execute decision

Observe: collect updated data

Evaluate: compare to expectation

Refine: adjust for next time

Examples

Smart Thermostat

Learns preferences. Each override = feedback.

PE: Adaptive Test Flow

Moves high-catch tests earlier based on observed fail patterns.

Key Takeaways

Without feedback, no learning.

Act-observe-refine is the engine of improvement.

Lesson 10: The Updated Environment

00:00.160 --> 00:05.760 Once agents have acted upon the environment, they observe its updated state. 00:06.200 --> 00:13.360 Their sensors receive new input data, which is then processed, analyzed, and used to improve the 00:13.400 --> 00:15.120 agent's future behavior.

Core Concept

After acting, the environment changes. Agent observes, compares, refines. Loop restarts.

Compounding Effect

1.01^365 = 37.78x improvement in one year

Key Takeaways

Learning is continuous and compounding.

An agent without feedback stagnates; with feedback it evolves.

Lesson 12: Key Characteristics of AI Agents

00:00.160 --> 00:08.480 An agent is defined as a system that perceives its environment through sensors and then acts upon that 00:08.480 --> 00:09.440 environment. 00:09.680 --> 00:17.240 But as agents become more advanced, their capabilities extend far beyond just perception and action.

Core Concept

Five universal characteristics define any AI agent's capability level.

Profile & Persona: Role, function, interaction style.

Memory: Context and knowledge retained across interactions.

Reasoning: Ability to analyze, conclude, solve.

Actions: What it does to achieve goals.

Learning: Ability to improve from feedback.

Key Takeaways

Every agent can be evaluated against these 5 traits.

Agent types differ by which characteristics are present and how sophisticated.

💡 From the Lecture
00:37.080 --> 00:44.440 Please remember that not all agent types must have all five characteristics to qualify as agents.
💡 From the Lecture
01:06.090 --> 01:13.410 The profile and persona description include details such as the agent's background, for example marketer 01:13.410 --> 01:15.250 or software engineer.

Lesson 13: Simple Reflex Agent

00:00.160 --> 00:06.320 The first type of agent structure will consider is the simple reflex agent. 00:07.040 --> 00:14.200 As one can infer from its name, this is a fundamental tool that reacts directly based on immediate 00:14.200 --> 00:15.080 perception.

Core Concept

Reacts to immediate perceptions with fixed rules. No memory, reasoning, or learning. IF

condition THEN action.

Examples

Thermostat

IF temp < 20C THEN heat ON. No adaptation.

PE: Limit Comparator

IF leakage > 100nA THEN FAIL. No lot context.

PE: Handler Alarm

IF jams > 5 THEN stop. No root cause reasoning.

Key Takeaways

Most basic form: perceive + react.

Works only for stable, predictable environments.

Recognizing these helps identify where to add intelligence.

Lesson 14: Model-based Reflex Agent

00:00.200 --> 00:05.640 The next agent type we'll explore is the model based reflex agent. 00:06.120 --> 00:12.200 Like simple reflex agents, these agents perceive their environment and act upon it. 00:12.720 --> 00:14.640 But there's a key distinction.

Core Concept

Adds internal model (memory/state) on top of rules. Handles partially observable environments.

Still rule-based, but with context.

Examples

Robot Vacuum

Maps room, tracks cleaned areas. Cannot learn dirty-area patterns.

PE: SPC Monitor

Tracks trends over lots, flags at +/-3 sigma. Fixed rules.

PE: Site Correlation Tracker

Maintains correlation model, flags deviations. Dynamic state, fixed rules.

Additional Context

Many semiconductor production systems ARE this type: track state, apply rules, but rules never

evolve without human intervention.

Key Takeaways

= simple reflex + memory/state.

Still rule-bound; no learning from outcomes.

Model updated by perception, NOT by success/failure.

💡 From the Lecture
01:23.950 --> 01:26.030 The difference is quite subtle.

Lesson 15: Goal-based Agent

00:00.160 --> 00:07.480 Whenever you use Google Maps or Waze, the application compares the estimated time it will take to reach 00:07.480 --> 00:14.000 your desired destination via different routes, and then recommends the fastest one.

Core Concept

Goes beyond reacting. Searches for action sequences that achieve a specific objective. Plans

ahead, evaluates options, picks the best path.

Key Difference

Reflex: 'What do I do NOW given this state?'

Goal-based: 'What sequence gets me to my GOAL?'

Key Points

Searches for action sequences aligned with objectives.

Can re-plan in real-time when conditions change.

Considers FUTURE states, not just current state.

Limitation: may over-optimize for one goal at expense of user experience.

Examples

Google Maps / Waze

Evaluates routes, recommends fastest. Adapts to traffic in real-time. May suggest

narrow/complicated routes because they are technically faster.

PE: Optimal Test Insertion

Goal = max coverage in min time. Searches orderings for best defect-catch sequence. May

suggest removing margin tests that serve long-term reliability.

PE: Qualification Planning

Plans stress test sequence (HTOL, UHAST, TCT) and sample sizes for min time. Adapts

when failures require re-evaluation.

Limitations

Does not weigh trade-offs between competing objectives (needs utility-based agent for

that).

Poorly defined goals = optimizing for the wrong thing (alignment problem).

Additional Context

In agentic AI, goal-based = planning modules:

LLM generating multi-step plans before executing

Search algorithms (A*, tree-of-thought)

ReAct/Plan-and-Execute patterns

Key Takeaways

Goal-based agents PLAN action sequences.

Adapt by re-planning when conditions change.

More capable than reflex but can over-optimize for single goals.

Lesson 16: Utility-based Agent

00:00.200 --> 00:06.920 The next type of agent we'll consider is a utility based agent in terms of sophistication. 00:07.200 --> 00:10.320 They rank higher compared to goal based agents. 00:10.800 --> 00:18.520 The reason is that utility based agents consider multiple factors to evaluate utility, rather than 00:18.520 --> 00:20.960 just achieving a predetermined goal.

Core Concept

A utility-based agent evaluates multiple competing factors simultaneously and selects the action

that maximizes overall 'utility' (a combined score). Unlike goal-based agents that ask 'does this

reach my goal?', utility-based agents ask 'what option gives me the BEST overall outcome across

ALL criteria?'

Key Difference from Goal-Based

Goal-based: 'Does this action achieve my target? Yes/No.'

Utility-based: 'Of all options, which one maximizes value across ALL factors I care about?'

Key Points

Considers multiple criteria simultaneously (not just one goal).

Weighs trade-offs between competing factors (return vs. risk, speed vs. quality).

Assigns a utility score to each option and picks the highest.

Leads to more nuanced, balanced decisions than pure goal-seeking.

Examples

Investment Agent (from lecture)

Does not simply seek return > 5%. Evaluates return, volatility, liquidity, and default risk

together. A higher-return security may be rejected if its volatility makes the risk-adjusted

utility lower than a safer option.

PE: Test Time vs. Coverage Trade-off

A goal-based agent would just maximize coverage. A utility-based agent weighs coverage,

test time cost, tester utilization, and risk of escapes. It might accept slightly lower

coverage if it dramatically reduces test time and cost.

PE: Disposition Decision

Instead of binary pass/fail, weighs: magnitude of shift, proximity to spec, lot history,

customer risk tolerance, cost of scrap vs. cost of field failure. Outputs the decision with

highest overall utility.

Additional Context

Utility-based agents solve the 'narrow optimization' problem of goal-based agents:

Goal-based: 'minimize test time' might sacrifice quality.

Utility-based: 'maximize [0.4*coverage + 0.3*speed + 0.2*cost_savings + 0.1*reliability]'

balances everything.

In agentic AI, this maps to:

Multi-criteria scoring in decision logic

Reward models in RLHF (balancing helpfulness, safety, truthfulness)

Weighted evaluation rubrics for agent output quality

Key Takeaways

Utility-based agents optimize across multiple dimensions simultaneously.

They handle trade-offs that goal-based agents cannot.

More realistic for complex real-world decisions where no single metric is sufficient.

The utility function defines what 'good' means; choosing it well is critical.

💡 From the Lecture
00:21.680 --> 00:23.640 Consider a simple example.
💡 From the Lecture
00:58.520 --> 01:06.800 For instance, a security with a 7% expected return might initially seem attractive, but suppose it 01:06.840 --> 01:08.840 carries high volatility.

Lesson 17: Learning Agent

00:00.080 --> 00:08.120 Learning agents possess the same capabilities as utility based and goal based agents, but are unique 00:08.120 --> 00:09.640 in their ability to learn. 00:09.880 --> 00:17.200 New experiences are added to their initial knowledge base, and as the agent gains experience, this 00:17.240 --> 00:24.040 enhances its ability to operate in unfamiliar environments and improve performance.

Core Concept

A learning agent can improve its own performance from experience. Unlike all previous types

(which operate on fixed logic regardless of outcomes), a learning agent refines its internal

model, decision rules, and strategies based on feedback. This is the most advanced agent type.

Key Difference from All Previous Types

All previous: Fixed logic. Performance on day 1000 = day 1 (unless human updates it).

Learning agent: Self-improving. Performance on day 1000 >> day 1 through accumulated

experience.

Key Points

Learns from experiences and adapts to unfamiliar environments.

Contains all standard components (environment, sensors, model, decision logic, actuators).

PLUS a learning element that refines the internal model based on feedback.

Continuously adapts and enhances performance over time.

This is what truly qualifies as 'intelligent' behavior.

Components of a Learning Agent

Performance Element: makes decisions and takes actions (like previous agent types)

Learning Element: observes feedback and modifies the performance element to improve

Critic: evaluates how well the agent is doing based on a fixed performance standard

Problem Generator: suggests exploratory actions to discover new knowledge

Examples

Self-improving recommendation system

Learns viewing preferences over time. Each interaction refines its taste model.

PE: Adaptive Guardbanding

Starts with conservative spec limits. Observes actual field returns and reliability data over

time. Gradually tightens or loosens limits based on real correlation between test

measurements and field performance. Gets better at predicting which devices will fail.

PE: Intelligent Yield Analysis

Agent that learns which process signatures correlate with yield loss. After seeing

hundreds of lots, it can predict yield issues from early process data before final test,

becoming more accurate with each new lot.

Additional Context

This is where modern AI truly lives:

LLMs improved via RLHF = learning agents (learn from human feedback)

Fine-tuned models = learning from domain-specific experience

Agents with memory that persist across sessions = accumulating experience

Self-reflection patterns (agent evaluates its own output and improves) = critic + learning

element

The full agent type hierarchy is now complete:

Simple Reflex < Model-Based Reflex < Goal-Based < Utility-Based < Learning Agent

Key Takeaways

Learning agents are the pinnacle: they improve themselves from experience.

The learning element is what separates true AI from automated systems.

All previous agent types are stepping stones to this level.

In practice, the best agents combine utility-based decision-making WITH learning.

Section 3 Complete - All agent types covered, from simple reflex to learning agents.

Lesson 18: Intro

00:00.160 --> 00:08.240 In the last lesson, we briefly touched on an essential aspect the learning abilities of AI agents. 00:08.920 --> 00:14.960 This is a central topic, and that's why we'll dedicate the next couple of lessons to it.

Core Concept

AI agents acquire knowledge through connections to external systems and human expertise.

This section explores the mechanisms that enable agents to learn, adapt, and improve over time

rather than remaining static tools with fixed knowledge.

Key Points

Knowledge acquisition is the foundation that transforms a static tool into an adaptive

agent

Agents enhance functionality by gathering relevant information from diverse sources

Integration of human expertise allows agents to make informed, context-rich decisions

Effective agents require proper model selection, prompt configuration, and guardrails

This bridges understanding agent types (Section 3) and building real systems

Key Difference from Section 3

Section 3 classified agent types by architecture. Section 4 focuses on how agents actually learn

and improve, regardless of their architecture. A Learning Agent (Section 3) needs the

mechanisms described here to actually function.

Examples

Lecture: An AI assistant that improves recommendations by learning user preferences

over time

PE: A test program agent that learns from engineer disposition decisions to auto-classify

future PDA outliers. Starts with rules, improves by absorbing the reasoning behind

human accept/reject calls.

Additional Context

In semiconductor PE, knowledge acquisition maps to how we train new engineers: read specs,

shadow experienced PEs, learn from past dispositions, build judgment. An AI agent follows the

same arc but at scale across thousands of lots. The 'guardrails' are critical: an agent making

disposition calls without proper bounds could release defective material or scrap good product.

Key Takeaways

1 Knowledge acquisition separates agents from static scripts

2 Two primary sources: human expertise and external data systems

3 Guardrails are essential in mission-critical domains like semiconductor qual

Lesson 19: Learning from Humans

00:00.240 --> 00:08.440 One of the most exciting aspects of AI agent systems is their ability to learn and continuously improve 00:08.440 --> 00:09.280 over time. 00:09.880 --> 00:13.200 To achieve this, they rely on three key sources.

Core Concept

AI agents learn from human feedback, corrections, preferences, and behavior patterns. This

human-in-the-loop learning creates a dynamic system where the agent continuously refines its

algorithms based on real expert input, becoming more efficient and contextually aware over

time.

Key Points

Human feedback (corrections, preferences, behavior patterns) directly refines agent

algorithms

Agents learn in real-time from interactions, creating a continuous improvement loop

Human knowledge integration enables better decisions than data alone

Human-AI collaboration: humans teach, agents scale that expertise

The agent amplifies human expertise, not replaces it

Learning Mechanisms

1 Corrections - Human corrects mistakes, agent updates its model

2 Preferences - Human selects preferred outcomes, agent learns ranking

3 Behavior patterns - Agent observes how humans handle situations, mimics approach

4 Explicit teaching - Human provides rules, context, or domain knowledge directly

Examples

Lecture: AI that learns from user corrections to improve response quality

PE - Corrections: PE overrides auto-bin. Agent learns: 'When Vout is marginal AND temp

coeff is in spec, pass the unit.'

PE - Preferences: PE consistently accepts 2-sigma outliers on non-critical params. Agent

learns this risk tolerance.

PE - Behavior: Agent observes PEs always check HTOL drift vs. pre-stress distribution

before dispositioning. Adopts this pattern.

Additional Context

This is essentially RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) applied to domain-

specific agents. In our world, the 'human feedback' is every disposition decision, rescreen call,

and limit adjustment. The challenge: different PEs have different risk tolerances. A well-designed

system captures reasoning (not just decisions) so the agent learns logic, not just patterns. This is

why ADMAP dispositions with clear justification are valuable as training data.

Key Takeaways

1 Human feedback is the highest-quality training signal for domain-specific agents

2 The agent amplifies human expertise, not replaces it

3 Quality of learning depends on quality of feedback - clear reasoning > raw decisions

4 Real-time learning enables continuous adaptation to shifting requirements

💡 From the Lecture
00:53.720 --> 00:59.680 This method is a viable learning source when other agents are employed for the same use case.
💡 From the Lecture
01:08.730 --> 01:16.410 Imagine a business deploying multiple customer support agents simultaneously across different regions.

Lesson 20: Learning from External Systems

00:00.360 --> 00:06.440 As previously noted, A.I. agents are autonomous in their decision making process. 00:06.760 --> 00:12.600 However, they require goals and predefined rules created by humans. 00:12.800 --> 00:20.400 One fundamental concept highlighting human influence throughout an AI agent's life cycle is known as 00:20.600 --> 00:23.240 human in the loop hittle.

Core Concept

AI agents learn from external data sources (datasets, APIs, web, other agents) and continuously

update their understanding. Unlike static tools with fixed knowledge, agents dynamically adapt

by synthesizing information from multiple external inputs in real-time.

Key Points

Agent-to-agent learning: share successful solutions, reducing human intervention

External data access: pull from datasets, web searches, APIs to enrich knowledge

Multi-source synthesis: combine data from multiple inputs for complete understanding

Dynamic vs. static: agents continuously update (unlike ChatGPT with fixed training

cutoff)

Agents identify when current knowledge is insufficient and seek additional sources

Three Learning Channels

1 From other agents - Shared solutions to common problems (collaborative intelligence)

2 From external data - APIs, databases, web sources (information gathering)

3 Multi-source synthesis - Combining inputs to form new understanding (reasoning)

Examples

Lecture: Customer support agent discovers fix, shares with all other agents instantly

Lecture: Surf-trip planner pulls weather APIs + surfing sites + tide data to predict optimal

week

PE - Agent-to-agent: One agent learns lot X failed from ESD at handler. Shares with all

agents monitoring that handler, preventing repeats.

PE - External data: Agent pulls STDF + SPC + maintenance logs to correlate yield

excursion with prober needle replacement.

PE - Synthesis: Combines historical PDA + reliability model + current distribution to

predict whether marginal unit survives HTOL.

Key Difference: Agents vs. Static AI Tools

Static tool (base ChatGPT): fixed knowledge cutoff. Agent: continuously pulls fresh data, learns

from new interactions, updates model. In PE terms: a static tool knows spec limits from the

datasheet. An agent knows spec limits AND last 6 months of SPC data AND current lot

distribution AND what happened to similar lots in reliability.

Additional Context

This describes the architecture behind a 'smart disposition system.' Today PEs manually pull

STDF, check SPC, review ADMAP history, cross-reference reliability data. An external-system-

learning agent automates this workflow: connects to all sources, synthesizes, presents (or

makes) the decision. Agent-to-agent learning is especially powerful for multi-site operations

where yield issues at one test floor immediately benefit all others.

Key Takeaways

1 External system access transforms agents from isolated tools to connected intelligence

2 Agent-to-agent learning enables collective knowledge without human bottlenecks

3 Multi-source synthesis is where real intelligence emerges (correlating disparate data)

4 Dynamic updating separates agents from static AI tools with fixed knowledge

💡 From the Lecture
00:42.560 --> 00:45.600 Consider a tech firm that builds the product.
💡 From the Lecture
01:41.990 --> 01:49.870 For instance, customer support staff actively update the chatbots knowledge base with new company policies 01:49.870 --> 01:52.230 and business specific practices.

Lesson 22: Distinguishing LLMs vs AI Workflows vs Agents (Agentic vs Non-agentic AI)

00:00.160 --> 00:03.360 Is ChatGPT an AI agent? 00:03.720 --> 00:07.040 Or what about an application connected to an LLM? 00:07.480 --> 00:09.320 Is that an AI agent? 00:10.000 --> 00:14.640 And what's the difference between an LLM and AI workflow?

Core Concept

Three distinct tiers exist in AI systems: raw LLMs (reactive text generators), AI workflows

(human-designed automation pipelines), and AI agents (autonomous, adaptive decision-

makers). Understanding where each sits on the autonomy spectrum is critical for choosing the

right tool.

Key Points

  • LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT) respond to prompts based on training data. They cannot act

independently, access external systems unprompted, or take initiative. They are contextually

aware only within their training corpus.

  • AI Workflows connect LLMs with external tools in a fixed sequence of steps. Example: an app

retrieves the latest email, sends it to an LLM for translation. The path is predefined by humans

and only activates on user request.

  • AI Agents overcome workflow limitations by acting autonomously. They initiate actions

without human intervention, reason about context, and adapt to their environment in real-time.

  • AI Agents can chain multiple actions: read an email requesting a meeting, check calendar

availability, consider weather, propose locations, all without being explicitly told each step.

  • Agents learn over time, remembering user preferences and adjusting behavior accordingly,

unlike static workflows that execute identically every time.

Key Difference

Workflow: Human designs the path, system follows it on command. Agent: System decides its

own path, acts proactively, and adapts.

Examples

LLM: You ask ChatGPT to translate text. It translates. It cannot check your email unless

you paste it in.

Workflow: App fetches your latest email automatically, sends to LLM for translation,

returns result. Fixed pipeline, no deviation.

Agent: Reads incoming email about a meeting request, checks your calendar, looks up

colleague's location via HR system, checks weather, books a cafe, sends invite. All

autonomous.

Additional Context

Our PDA Review skill is an interesting hybrid. Its step-by-step structure (gather files, scan, group,

dispose) is a fixed workflow. But its ML prediction model, anomaly detection, and training

feedback loop give it genuine cross-session learning, pushing it beyond a pure workflow toward

agent-like adaptability. The workflow is rigid; the intelligence within each step is not.

Key Takeaways

LLMs are powerful but passive; they only respond when prompted

Workflows automate sequences but cannot deviate from their designed path

Agents combine autonomy + reasoning + adaptability for truly independent operation

Most real-world systems are hybrids along this spectrum, not pure categories

💡 From the Lecture
00:10.000 --> 00:14.640 And what's the difference between an LLM and AI workflow?
💡 From the Lecture
00:30.760 --> 00:37.320 It's essentially a chat interface with a large language model on top of it serving as its engine.

Lesson 23: How AI Agents Reason and Act (ReAct)

00:00.120 --> 00:05.160 Setting up an in-person meeting can involve more steps than you might expect. 00:05.440 --> 00:07.280 Here's what usually happens. 00:07.520 --> 00:11.160 Your business associate suggests meeting face to face.

Core Concept

ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) is a framework where agents alternate between thinking through a

problem and executing actions based on that reasoning. Each action's result feeds back into the

next reasoning step, creating an adaptive loop.

Key Points

  • ReAct agents follow a structured cycle: Reason about the situation, then Act on that

reasoning, then Observe the result, then Reason again with new information.

  • Meeting setup example: Agent reasons it needs calendar data, acts by checking the calendar,

observes availability, reasons about location preferences, acts by checking HR system for

colleague's work status, and so on.

  • Each observation can change the agent's plan. If the cafe is booked, the agent reasons about

alternatives and acts accordingly. This is adaptive planning.

  • ReAct agents can integrate multiple tool calls: calendar APIs, HR software, weather services,

restaurant booking systems, email/messaging platforms.

  • The pattern significantly reduces human effort by handling the entire chain of decisions and

actions that would otherwise require back-and-forth coordination.

Key Difference

ReAct is observation-dependent: each action's output directly influences the next reasoning

step. The plan evolves in real-time based on what the agent discovers.

Examples

Business meeting setup: Agent checks calendar (act), sees Tuesday is free (observe),

checks if colleague is on-site (act), learns they're remote (observe), pivots to suggesting

a video call instead of a cafe (reason + act).

The agent can even handle voice-activated reservations and send calendar

invites/emails autonomously after making all decisions.

Key Takeaways

ReAct = interleaved reasoning and action with real-time feedback

Highly flexible: adapts plan based on each observation

Trade-off: can be distracted by irrelevant information encountered during actions

💡 From the Lecture
00:33.640 --> 00:39.480 If the weather's good, but you remember it was pretty crowded last time, so you'll have to double 00:39.480 --> 00:41.000 check if there's space.

Lesson 24: How AI Agents Reason without Observation (ReWoo)

00:00.200 --> 00:07.920 The other critical framework used for designing AI agents is called Riwu, which stands for reasoning 00:07.920 --> 00:09.720 without observation. 00:10.200 --> 00:17.680 With Riwu, we instruct the agent to plan all necessary steps, ensuring it's not influenced by tool 00:17.680 --> 00:19.520 outputs for action planning.

Core Concept

ReWoo (Reasoning Without Observation) is a framework where the agent plans ALL steps

upfront before executing any of them. Unlike ReAct, tool outputs during execution do not

influence the action plan.

Key Points

  • The agent creates a complete action plan first: check calendar, confirm work location via HR,

verify cafe availability, identify backup location, all outlined before any execution begins.

  • Execution follows the plan sequentially without deviation. The agent does not adjust mid-

stream based on intermediate results.

  • Advantage: avoids distractions. A ReAct agent might get sidetracked by a special offer on a

cafe's website; a ReWoo agent sticks to its predetermined steps.

  • Disadvantage: rigidity. If the cafe is fully booked (unexpected result), the ReWoo agent may

struggle to adapt quickly since deviation from plan wasn't accounted for.

  • Best suited for predictable tasks where the sequence of steps is well-understood and unlikely

to require mid-course changes.

Key Difference

ReAct: Plan-act-observe-replan (adaptive). ReWoo: Plan everything first, then execute

sequentially (deterministic).

Examples

ReWoo meeting setup: Agent plans 5 steps upfront (check calendar, check HR, book

cafe, identify backup, send invites), then executes them in order regardless of

intermediate findings.

If step 3 fails (cafe booked), step 4 (backup location) was already planned. But if ALL

options fail, the rigid plan has no recovery mechanism built in.

Key Takeaways

ReWoo = full plan upfront, execute without deviation

Focused and efficient for predictable tasks

Brittle when unexpected situations arise mid-execution

Choose ReAct for dynamic environments, ReWoo for stable/predictable ones

💡 From the Lecture
02:18.110 --> 02:25.790 Of course, both frameworks have their pros and cons and are preferable in different AI agent use cases.

Lesson 25: Single Agents

00:00.120 --> 00:07.160 Whenever we discuss AI agent systems, it's essential to be aware of whether the workflow involves a 00:07.160 --> 00:11.760 single AI agent or multiple AI agents working together.

Core Concept

A single-agent system uses one AI agent equipped with multiple tools to handle a range of tasks.

Simplicity of architecture does not limit capability; adding tools expands what the agent can do.

Key Points

  • Single agent systems are simpler to build, debug, and manage than multi-agent systems. They

are the ideal starting point for AI implementation.

  • Power comes from tool integration, not agent count. One agent with access to email,

calendar, booking, and messaging tools can handle complex workflows independently.

  • Example: a personal assistant agent that responds to emails, books venues, schedules

meetings, and manages communications, all as a single unified system.

  • Single agents maintain full context across all their tasks since everything runs through one

reasoning process. No inter-agent communication overhead.

  • Understanding single agents is foundational before moving to multi-agent architectures.

Key Takeaways

Start simple: one agent + many tools is powerful and manageable

Tool integration is the primary scaling mechanism for single agents

No communication overhead; full context maintained naturally

💡 From the Lecture
00:54.560 --> 00:59.440 This represents an AI use case involving a single AI agent.

Lesson 26: Multi-agents

00:00.080 --> 00:05.360 When you're part of a team, you don't expect everyone to take on each other's roles. 00:05.480 --> 00:10.440 Do you suppose your company wants to redesign its website homepage? 00:10.720 --> 00:18.640 You need a graphic designer, a copywriter, a marketing specialist, a brand manager, and an SEO consultant.

Core Concept

Multi-agent systems use multiple specialized agents that collaborate, delegate, and

communicate to handle complex tasks that exceed what a single agent can efficiently manage

alone.

Key Points

  • Each agent specializes in a domain (scheduling, research, communication, analysis), enabling

deeper expertise per task area compared to one generalist agent.

  • Agents communicate and delegate: a coordinator agent may assign sub-tasks to specialist

agents, then synthesize their outputs into a final result.

  • Parallel execution is possible: multiple agents can work simultaneously on independent sub-

tasks, reducing total completion time.

  • Trade-offs include communication overhead, coordination complexity, potential for

conflicting actions, and harder debugging compared to single-agent systems.

  • Multi-agent systems shine for complex, multi-domain tasks where no single agent can hold all

necessary context or tools efficiently.

Key Difference

Single agent: One brain, many tools, full context. Multi-agent: Many brains, specialized roles,

requires coordination protocol.

Examples

Event planning: one agent handles venue research, another manages invitations, a third

coordinates schedules. A supervisor agent orchestrates the overall workflow.

Software development: a coding agent writes code, a review agent checks quality, a

testing agent validates functionality, a deployment agent handles releases.

Key Takeaways

Specialization enables deeper expertise per domain

Coordination overhead is the main cost of multi-agent systems

Use multi-agent when task complexity exceeds single-agent capacity

Start with single agent, scale to multi-agent only when needed

Lesson 28: How to Implement AI Agents in Your Business

00:09.480 --> 00:12.600 First, you need to define clear objectives. 00:12.720 --> 00:16.760 Understand well what you want to achieve with AI agents. 00:17.360 --> 00:19.360 Why does your business need this tool?

Core Concept

Deploying AI agents in a business setting requires a structured approach: define objectives first,

ensure data quality, choose the right agent architecture, iterate based on user experience,

monitor KPIs, and maintain human oversight.

Key Points

  • Define Clear Objectives: What does success look like? (e.g., enhance customer satisfaction,

reduce operational costs). Clear goals create a roadmap for implementation.

  • Data Quality: High-quality, reliable data must flow seamlessly from existing systems to

support the agent's knowledge base. Garbage in = garbage out.

  • Agent Structure Selection: Match complexity to the task. Simple reflex agent for basic tasks;

learning agent for complex, changing environments.

  • User Experience: Once a prototype exists, observe how end users actually interact with it.

Refine instructions based on real usage patterns.

  • Performance Monitoring: After deployment, track KPIs continuously to ensure the agent

meets its objectives.

  • Human Oversight: AI agents can operate independently, but complex or sensitive tasks may

require human intervention as a safety net.

Additional Context

This maps directly to how we might build a new ChipAgents skill: define the goal (e.g., automate

PDA dispositions), ensure good training data (prior reports), choose architecture (workflow with

ML components), test with real users, monitor accuracy, and keep human review in the loop.

💡 From the Lecture
01:32.120 --> 01:38.480 This use case requires a learning agent who can adapt to a rapidly changing environment.
💡 From the Lecture
02:20.640 --> 02:28.120 It's important to have clear rules about when and how people should step in, especially for more complex 02:28.120 --> 02:29.640 or sensitive tasks.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:20.640 --> 02:28.120 It's important to have clear rules about when and how people should step in, especially for more complex 02:28.120 --> 02:29.640 or sensitive tasks.
  • 02:30.040 --> 02:32.920 We'll explore this topic further in later lessons.

Lesson 29: Select a Model

00:00.160 --> 00:06.960 There are dozens of major lmes and hundreds more that are noteworthy for various reasons. 00:07.640 --> 00:12.040 So which one should you choose to power your AI agent? 00:12.520 --> 00:15.040 The smartest or most sophisticated one?

Core Concept

Model selection is a balancing act between task complexity, performance requirements, cost,

and speed. Start with the most capable model, establish a baseline, then explore whether

simpler models can match that quality.

Key Points

  • Evaluate Task Complexity: Simple tasks (FAQ, basic intent) can use smaller/cheaper models.

Complex reasoning tasks need advanced models.

  • Complex Models: Excel at intricate problems but come with higher cost and longer processing

time.

  • Simpler Models: Faster and cheaper, suitable when high-level reasoning isn't required.
  • Prototyping Strategy: Always prototype with the BEST model first. This sets the quality ceiling.

Then test if cheaper models can match that output.

  • Cyclical Evaluation: Continuously assess performance against designated tasks. Model

selection isn't a one-time decision.

  • Balance: Accuracy vs. speed vs. cost vs. scalability. No single model wins on all axes.

Key Takeaways

Start expensive/capable, then optimize down once you know what 'good' looks like

Task complexity is the primary driver of model choice

Re-evaluate as models improve and costs change over time

💡 From the Lecture
00:22.040 --> 00:28.320 Different models come with different strengths, so it's important to factor that into your decision.
💡 From the Lecture
00:48.400 --> 00:56.280 Not every use case requires the most advanced model for straightforward tasks, like quickly answering 00:56.280 --> 01:00.040 common FAQs or identifying user intent.

Lesson 30: External Tools the Agent Can Use

00:00.160 --> 00:04.200 Agents need tools to communicate with other software. 00:04.920 --> 00:11.880 APIs frequently play this role and create a bridge between agents and the different software they work 00:11.880 --> 00:12.320 with.

Core Concept

AI agents interact with external systems primarily through APIs. Their tools fall into two

categories: Data Tools (retrieve information) and Action Tools (perform operations).

Key Points

  • APIs are the primary bridge between agents and software systems. They allow efficient,

structured data retrieval and submission.

  • Without APIs, agents must mimic human interactions (e.g., scraping UIs), which is error-prone

and fragile.

  • Data Tools: Retrieve information needed for decisions. Examples: query a customer database,

search the web, look up product details.

  • Action Tools: Perform operations that change state. Examples: schedule meetings, open

support tickets, process refunds, send emails.

  • Both tool types together enable autonomous operation: the agent gathers context (data

tools) then acts on it (action tools).

Key Difference

Data Tools: Read-only, information gathering. Action Tools: Write/execute, state-changing

operations.

💡 From the Lecture
00:48.320 --> 00:55.080 For example, a data tool can check information about a given customer in the database, or it can read 00:55.080 --> 00:55.800 a PDF.
Key Takeaways
  • 00:56.440 --> 01:00.960 Another data tool can search for information on Google and so on.
  • 01:01.560 --> 01:08.760 The common aspect between these operations is that they help agents retrieve information, which is 01:08.760 --> 01:12.080 necessary for executing the agent's planned tasks.
  • 01:12.400 --> 01:20.840 The second type is action tools, which allow agents to perform specific tasks and take actions such 01:20.840 --> 01:26.840 as scheduling meetings, opening customer support tickets, or handling refund requests.
  • 01:27.360 --> 01:33.680 Agents need these action tools to change the environment and accomplish their intended goals.

Lesson 31: Configuring Instructions and Prompt Engineering Best Practices

00:00.080 --> 00:07.480 You're likely already aware how crucial prompt engineering is when working with large language models. 00:08.080 --> 00:12.080 Just a few years ago, the term was virtually unknown.

Practices

Core Concept

The quality of an agent's output is directly proportional to the clarity and specificity of its

instructions. Prompt engineering is the discipline of crafting those instructions effectively.

Key Points

  • Clear and Concise Instructions: Reduce ambiguity to get higher quality outputs. Vague

prompts produce vague results.

  • LLM-Friendly Routines: Use existing documents to build a robust knowledge base. Give the

agent context it needs for accurate responses.

  • Break Down Complex Tasks: Simplify multi-step processes to avoid exceeding the model's

context window and prevent cascading errors.

  • Define Explicit Actions: Never use vague directives. Outline specific steps the agent should

take in each scenario.

  • Capture Edge Cases Proactively: Brainstorm unusual scenarios upfront. Example: what should

the agent do for a refund request that falls outside normal parameters?

Key Takeaways

Specificity > brevity when writing agent instructions

Edge cases are where agents fail most; anticipate them in advance

Instructions are living documents; refine post-deployment based on real failures

💡 From the Lecture
01:48.430 --> 01:54.430 For example, rather than giving your agent vague instructions like help the customer with their order 01:54.430 --> 02:01.670 issue, provide explicit and actionable instructions such as if a customer reports their order hasn't 02:01.670 --> 02:07.190 arrived, ask immediately for their order ID and check the delivery status.
💡 From the Lecture
02:12.750 --> 02:18.230 Lastly, we should always make an effort to consider and capture edge cases.

Lesson 32: Few-shot Prompting

00:00.360 --> 00:06.440 Are you familiar with the concepts of zero shot, one shot, and few shot prompting? 00:12.800 --> 00:18.720 Understanding these prompting techniques will help you when configuring AI agent systems.

Core Concept

Prompting techniques exist on a spectrum from zero examples to extensive training. The right

technique depends on how much guidance the agent needs to perform reliably.

Key Points

  • Zero-Shot Prompting: No examples provided. The model relies entirely on pre-existing

knowledge. Like a new sales rep on day one with no onboarding.

  • One-Shot Prompting: One example provided alongside instructions. Like watching your

manager serve one client, then handling the rest alone.

  • Few-Shot Prompting: 2-10 examples provided. The manager serves several clients while you

observe, giving you templates for multiple scenarios.

  • Fine-Tuning: Beyond few-shot (many examples + structured guidance). Like weeks of

intensive role-playing and performance review. This trains the model itself, not just prompts it.

  • Selection matters: Just as a sales rep's performance varies with training quality, an agent's

effectiveness depends heavily on the prompting strategy chosen.

Key Difference

Prompting (zero/one/few-shot): Guides behavior at inference time, no model changes. Fine-

tuning: Permanently modifies the model's weights through extensive training.

💡 From the Lecture
00:23.720 --> 00:30.920 Prompting essentially means asking an LLM to perform a task without giving it any examples.
💡 From the Lecture
02:38.760 --> 02:46.440 Selecting the optimal method ensures the agent consistently delivers accurate results in real world 02:46.440 --> 02:47.520 applications.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:18.560 --> 02:22.800 This analogy applies directly to configuring AI agents.
  • 02:23.160 --> 02:29.440 Just as a sales representatives, performance can vary significantly depending on the amount of training 02:29.440 --> 02:30.240 provided.
  • 02:30.560 --> 02:38.320 The effectiveness of AI agents depends heavily on the prompting strategy or fine tuning used.
  • 02:38.760 --> 02:46.440 Selecting the optimal method ensures the agent consistently delivers accurate results in real world 02:46.440 --> 02:47.520 applications.

Lesson 33: Chain of Thought Reasoning

00:00.160 --> 00:01.360 Chain of thought. 00:01.400 --> 00:09.840 Cot is a prompt engineering technique that asks AI models to explain their reasoning and list the intermediate 00:09.840 --> 00:12.680 steps used to arrive at a conclusion.

Core Concept

Chain of Thought (CoT) is a prompting technique that asks the model to explain its reasoning

step-by-step before giving a final answer. This improves accuracy on complex tasks and makes

the agent's logic transparent and debuggable.

Key Points

  • Without CoT: 'Best month to visit Greece on a budget for beaches?' Answer: 'September.' No

explanation, no way to verify reasoning.

  • With CoT: Model lists beach months (May-Sep), eliminates expensive months (Jun-Aug),

compares remaining (May vs Sep on weather), concludes September. Transparent and

verifiable.

  • Performance Boost: Research shows agents perform significantly better on complex tasks

when they articulate intermediate reasoning steps.

  • Transparency: CoT lets engineers see WHY the agent reached a conclusion, making it far

easier to identify and correct errors in logic.

  • Debugging: When an agent makes a mistake with CoT enabled, you can pinpoint exactly

which reasoning step went wrong rather than guessing.

Key Takeaways

CoT = 'show your work' for AI models

Critical for complex multi-step reasoning tasks

Enables human verification and targeted correction of agent logic

Lesson 34: Guardrails

00:00.120 --> 00:03.200 Why do we need guardrails on roads? 00:03.560 --> 00:06.560 They prevent cars from veering off cliffs. 00:06.600 --> 00:07.120 Right. 00:07.880 --> 00:11.000 This approach reduces the risk for drivers.

Core Concept

Just as road safety requires multiple layered mechanisms (guardrails, speed limits, traffic lights,

signs), AI agent safety requires multiple specialized guardrails working together to mitigate

different risks.

Key Points

  • No single mechanism provides sufficient protection. Multiple specialized guardrails together

create a robust system.

  • Information Security: Prevent the agent from inadvertently revealing sensitive or confidential

information.

  • Brand Alignment: Ensure the agent's behavior consistently reflects company tone and culture.

Misalignment harms reputation.

  • Accuracy: Prevent hallucinations and incorrect answers through verification mechanisms.
  • OpenAI's recommended heuristics: (a) Prioritize data privacy and content safety. (b) Add

guardrails based on real-world edge cases and failures. (c) Balance security with user

experience.

  • Guardrails are iterative: as more real-world data becomes available post-deployment,

additional layers are added continuously.

Key Takeaways

Layered defense: no single guardrail is enough

Guardrails evolve with real-world usage data

Security vs. UX is a constant balancing act

💡 From the Lecture
02:19.330 --> 02:25.530 As more information becomes available after the agent is deployed in real world settings, additional 02:25.530 --> 02:27.650 layers of guardrails will be added.
💡 From the Lecture
02:40.410 --> 02:46.330 Second, add new guardrails based on real world edge cases and failures.

Lesson 35: The Importance of Human Intervention

00:00.320 --> 00:07.280 In the previous lesson, we didn't cover one of the most important safeguards for reducing risk when 00:07.280 --> 00:08.920 launching an AI agent. 00:09.240 --> 00:12.320 I'm talking about human intervention.

Core Concept

Human oversight is the most important safeguard when deploying AI agents, especially early on.

Humans catch subtle issues that automated tests miss, and agents should escalate to humans

when uncertain.

Key Points

  • Human intervention is especially critical early in deployment when the agent's failure modes

are still being discovered.

  • Humans have unparalleled intuition and common sense for identifying subtle failures, edge

cases, and areas for improvement that automated tests miss.

  • Human oversight acts as a vital feedback mechanism for spotting subtle inaccuracies.
  • Developers can implement escalation mechanisms: when the agent isn't confident in its

answer, it hands off to a human.

  • In customer service: escalate to a human agent. In coding: hand control back to the user. The

pattern is universal across domains.

Key Takeaways
  • 00:39.760 --> 00:46.960 Human oversight acts as a vital feedback mechanism, allowing us to spot subtle inaccuracies.
  • 00:47.480 --> 00:54.240 Additionally, an AI agent's developers can implement a human intervention mechanism, which means involving 00:54.240 --> 01:00.240 humans as soon as the agent is not certain if it's providing the best possible answer.
  • 01:00.800 --> 01:05.680 In customer service, this involves escalating the issue to a human agent.
  • 01:06.040 --> 01:11.920 While for a coding agent, this entails handing control back to the user.

Lesson 36: How to Evaluate AI Agents

00:05.240 --> 00:11.280 Put simply, we'll ask what makes an AI agent good or effective? 00:16.960 --> 00:20.720 Is a good agent the one that responds faster? 00:21.520 --> 00:22.120 Sure. 00:22.480 --> 00:26.520 But what if those fast responses are incorrect?

Core Concept

A good AI agent must balance multiple criteria: accuracy, speed, coherence, cost, and safety.

The priority weighting depends on the agent's purpose. Metrics alone won't catch every issue;

real-world user experience reveals problems that numbers miss.

Key Points

  • Five evaluation dimensions: Accuracy, Speed, Coherence, Cost, Safety. No agent can maximize

all simultaneously.

  • Context determines priorities: A customer service chatbot prioritizes coherence and safety.

An autonomous trading agent prioritizes accuracy and speed.

  • Real-world example: A real estate chatbot was technically accurate but users didn't trust it

because it sounded robotic and repetitive. No metric captured this.

  • The fix wasn't better accuracy; it was improving tone, memory, and contextual awareness.

User engagement improved dramatically after.

  • Key lesson: Metrics are essential, but user experience reveals issues that metrics alone often

overlook.

  • Evaluation is iterative: expect several iterations across multiple aspects. Use data-driven

decisions to identify strengths and hidden weaknesses.

Key Takeaways

Evaluation criteria must align with the agent's specific purpose and context

Technical correctness alone doesn't guarantee user trust or adoption

Combine quantitative metrics with qualitative user feedback

Iterate: evaluation is ongoing, not a one-time gate

💡 From the Lecture
01:48.250 --> 01:50.610 Consider a real world example.
💡 From the Lecture
03:00.090 --> 03:08.770 The key lesson metrics are essential, but user experience reveals issues that metrics alone often overlook.

Lesson 47: Cloud Services

00:00.120 --> 00:07.440 Saying that AI agents require significant computing resources would be an understatement. 00:07.800 --> 00:14.240 The more advanced your agent becomes, and the more tasks it handles, the greater its computing demands 00:14.240 --> 00:14.920 will be.

Core Concept

Saying that AI agents require significant computing resources would be an understatement. The more advanced your agent becomes, and the more tasks it handles, the greater its computing demands will be. If you run a business, this can be seen as another make versus buy decision.

Key Points

  • If you opt for make, you'll need to purchase hardware that can handle peak usage and ensure you have sufficient GPUs for heavy AI computations.
  • Alternatively, buy means using an external service that provides flexibility and doesn't require a significant upfront investment.
  • Cloud solutions provide scalable infrastructure, enabling you to experiment freely and pay only for the computing power your AI agents utilize.
  • You don't need to buy expensive hardware upfront that may not be used for significant portions of the time with cloud services.
  • You can handle peak loads and then pay much less at times when you don't use the service as intensively.
  • The three major cloud providers Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud Platform offer robust solutions tailored explicitly for AI workloads.
  • They provide powerful GPUs, extensive storage, integrated APIs, and comprehensive tools to streamline the development and deployment of AI agents.

Lesson 54: Agentic Workflows vs. AI Agents

Core Concept

At the beginning of our journey, it would be beneficial to make a crucial distinction between AI workflows and AI agents. Workflows are systems that utilize Llms in predefined code paths. Agents, on the other hand, enable Llms to independently decide how to approach tasks and select the appropriate tools.

Key Points

  • When it comes to workflows, the system follows a set of predefined steps each time it runs.
  • Programmers design this sequence in advance, and the model is expected to operate strictly within those parameters.
  • The LLM serves as one component within a larger structured pipeline.
  • But what does this look like in practice?
  • Imagine adding a chatbot to your website designed to help customers find the right product.
  • When a visitor asks for a specific type of item, their message is sent to an LLM connected to your product database.
  • The MLM then searches for the most matches and returns a predefined response.
  • In this setup, the chatbot follows a fixed structured path.

Lesson 56: When (and when not) to Use AI Agents

Core Concept

The primary function of this course is designing practical and functional AI agents. But before diving into AI agent design patterns, it's crucial to consider when an agentic approach is essential. Let's take a moment to address this topic.

Key Points

  • Building an agentic workflow is most appropriate when the required steps are clearly defined.
  • This typically applies to well-structured projects where the path to the solution is already known.
  • If you have a clear understanding of what needs to be done, it's easy to outline the necessary steps and program a sequence of predefined actions with confidence.
  • This is a much simpler solution compared to building an agent.
  • The reward for this simplicity is faster response times and lower computational costs.
  • Both factors are critical when deploying an AI product in the real world.
  • After all, you wouldn't want customers waiting several minutes just to receive a product recommendation, would you?
  • In fact, AI research firm anthropic notes that in many situations, optimizing a single LLM call is the most effective approach.

Lesson 59: General Principles of Prompt Structuring

00:05.680 --> 00:12.120 One of the most critical aspects when designing single agent systems is how you'll structure their system 00:12.120 --> 00:12.760 prompt. 00:13.080 --> 00:21.360 It acts as the agent's foundational instruction set, defining its personality, role, tone, and limitations.

Core Concept

One of the most critical aspects when designing single agent systems is how you'll structure their system prompt. It acts as the agent's foundational instruction set, defining its personality, role, tone, and limitations. It's essentially the blueprint that shapes how the agent interprets user input and generates responses.

Key Points

  • The lens through which it perceives the world.
  • This goes far beyond a mere technical detail.
  • The way you structure the system prompt has a direct impact on the agent's overall performance.
  • Sometimes you'll find that minor tweaks can lead to considerable improvements.
  • Here are a few general principles that are recommended in OpenAI's prompt engineering guide.
  • The more clearly you define the agent's role, the better its output will be.
  • Vague role definitions had little value or specialization, which means the agent's responses will lack precision.
  • Secondly, clearly state the desired result to the agent.

Lesson 60: Prompting Frameworks

00:14.760 --> 00:20.400 Depending on the amount of context or prior guidance the model needs to perform a task. 00:20.640 --> 00:28.480 You can opt for zero shot, prompting one shot prompting and few shot, prompting the apparent trade 00:28.520 --> 00:29.440 off when choosing.

Core Concept

In this lesson, we'll talk about a few essential prompt engineering techniques that will help you when configuring AI agent systems. Depending on the amount of context or prior guidance the model needs to perform a task. You can opt for zero shot, prompting one shot prompting and few shot, prompting the apparent trade off when choosing.

Key Points

  • A prompting technique is between the size and complexity of the prompt and the model's performance.
  • Zero shot prompting essentially means asking an LLM to perform a task without giving it any examples.
  • Instead, the model relies on its pre-existing knowledge to provide an appropriate response when you interact with an LLM, without providing any examples of how it should respond, you're using zero shot prompting.
  • This makes the prompt much more concise, simple, and faster to create, but will probably lead to less accurate results.
  • The likelihood of getting an undesired output rises sharply when you haven't shown the model what the desired result should look like.
  • So what happens if we give the agent just one example.
  • That's the idea behind one shot prompting.
  • It combines instructions with a single example to show the Lem what the desired output should look like.
💡 From the Lecture
00:37.000 --> 00:44.240 Zero shot prompting essentially means asking an LLM to perform a task without giving it any examples.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:16.600 --> 02:17.640 Window size.
  • 02:18.680 --> 02:24.160 Typically, you should use more examples and check for context window issues.
  • 02:24.480 --> 02:31.240 If such limitations exist, the number of examples can be reduced until you find the right balance between 02:31.240 --> 02:34.600 the provided examples and the agent's performance.
  • 02:35.040 --> 02:41.360 In some instances, if the task at hand is simple, you can opt for zero shot prompting.

Lesson 61: Positive and Negative Prompting

00:05.520 --> 00:11.880 When working with AI models, examples are one of the most effective tools for improving results. 00:12.240 --> 00:14.960 They show the model exactly what you want. 00:15.280 --> 00:21.240 But another technique can improve results, adding do and don't instructions.

Core Concept

When working with AI models, examples are one of the most effective tools for improving results. They show the model exactly what you want. But another technique can improve results, adding do and don't instructions.

Key Points

  • The do and don't commands are about providing the model with facts.
  • They define how it should behave when generating a response to your prompt.
  • Positive prompting involves instructing the model on what to do.
  • Think of it as giving the model green lights signals that highlight the qualities or structures you want it to include.
  • For example, use a friendly conversational tone.
  • Organize the response into numbered steps.
  • The more specific you are, the less the model has to guess.
  • Here are some due instructions from one of our projects.

Lesson 62: Chain-of-Thought (CoT)

00:05.600 --> 00:06.680 Chain of thought. 00:06.720 --> 00:14.360 Cot is a prompt engineering technique that instructs AI models to explain their reasoning and outline 00:14.360 --> 00:17.560 the immediate steps they take to reach a conclusion.

Core Concept

Chain of thought. Cot is a prompt engineering technique that instructs AI models to explain their reasoning and outline the immediate steps they take to reach a conclusion. If you ask an LLM, which is the best month to visit Greece?

Key Points

  • If I enjoy going to the beach but have a limited budget, the response could be September.
  • This answers the question we asked, but does not provide additional details.
  • With chain of thought reasoning, the system must explain its reasoning so it may respond in the following way.
  • If you enjoy going to the beach, then the months in which you can do that in Greece are May, June, July, August and September.
  • The prices in June, July and August are significantly higher compared to the beginning and the end of the season.
  • So we're left with May and September, but the chances of getting more sunny days in late September are higher compared to May.
  • Therefore, the best option is to book September.
  • Okay, AI researchers have found that agents perform better when they articulate their reasoning steps, particularly in complex tasks.
Key Takeaways
  • 01:10.520 --> 01:13.760 Therefore, the best option is to book September.
  • 01:14.480 --> 01:21.920 Okay, AI researchers have found that agents perform better when they articulate their reasoning steps, 01:21.960 --> 01:24.480 particularly in complex tasks.
  • 01:25.080 --> 01:32.120 Another important observation is that chain of thought reasoning increases transparency, allowing AI 01:32.120 --> 01:39.720 engineers who build agentic systems to understand the reasoning of agents and correct it if necessary.
  • 01:40.280 --> 01:46.680 If agents commit errors, it becomes much easier to identify these mistakes and correct them.

Lesson 64: The Augmented LLM

Core Concept

As mentioned earlier, the augmented LM serves as the fundamental building block of Agentic systems. Here's the core idea behind it. An LM is powerful on its own, but it becomes even more impressive when augmented with retrieval systems, external tools, and memory capabilities.

Key Points

  • Retrieval allows the model to search external data that wasn't included in its training and gain access to it.
  • Tools, on the other hand, allow the model to access external APIs that perform specialized tasks such as currency conversion calculations, weather forecasting, language translation, sending messages, or even booking reservations.
  • And finally, memory is what enables the LM to retain knowledge over time and recall user preferences so it doesn't have to start from scratch in every future interaction.
  • A user owns 100 Apple shares, which they purchased at $175 per share on July 1st.
  • They have access to an augmented LM, which has been specifically equipped with memory retrieval and tool capabilities, allowing it to answer specific portfolio questions for the user.

  • In step one, the model accesses memory to retrieve the user's personal investment data.

Lesson 65: Prompt Chaining

Core Concept

Sometimes the challenge you bring to gen AI is too large for an LLM to handle in one go. Picture an entrepreneur trying to generate a comprehensive business plan with AI, or a marketing executive developing a complex omnichannel campaign. Or consider a student seeking an accurate, detailed summary of a 300 page textbook.

Key Points

  • In all these cases, we cannot expect an LLM to be capable of solving such large tasks simultaneously.
  • Instead, we should break down the enormous task into smaller and digestible steps.
  • We refer to this approach as prompt chaining.
  • The first order of business is to break down the process into smaller, manageable tasks organized in a clear and logical sequence.
  • Then when the user activates the sequence with their query.
  • Each step of the LM call processes the output of the previous step.
  • So in practice, when a marketing executive asks for a comprehensive campaign plan, we have the following.
  • Starting from the executive's query, the first LM creates a campaign brief and outlines key action items.

Lesson 68: Orchestrator-worker

00:05.720 --> 00:11.040 As workflows become more sophisticated, they also exhibit greater flexibility. 00:19.080 --> 00:25.720 A typical feature of this structure is the presence of an LM orchestrator or planner, which receives 00:25.720 --> 00:33.360 the user query, breaks it down into several subtasks, delegates those subtasks to other LMS, and 00:33.360 --> 00:37.560 then submits their outputs to a synthesizer LM.

Core Concept

As workflows become more sophisticated, they also exhibit greater flexibility. One such example of this is the orchestrator worker workflow, which we'll examine in this lesson. A typical feature of this structure is the presence of an LM orchestrator or planner, which receives the user query, breaks it down into several subtasks, delegates those subtasks to other LMS, and then submits their outputs to a synthesizer LM.

Key Points

  • This workflow is used when the number of subtasks that need to be performed cannot be predicted in advance.
  • This is precisely what differentiates it from the parallelization process we just saw in the previous lesson.
  • In parallelization, tasks are predefined and static, whereas the orchestrator worker workflow dynamically creates its tasks.
  • As a result, the latter is considerably more sophisticated.
  • So why is this still considered a workflow?
  • Although the LM orchestrator determines the optimal approach to solve a problem, this process still follows a precise and repeatable sequence.
  • We break down a primary task into smaller subtasks, assign each to specialized worker LMS for execution, and then use a synthesizer LM to integrate their outputs into a cohesive result.
  • So in what type of situations is this workflow used in practice?
💡 From the Lecture
01:39.530 --> 01:44.690 So in what type of situations is this workflow used in practice?
💡 From the Lecture
02:01.250 --> 02:07.650 Consider a scenario where you want to apply this workflow to the development of software applications.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:32.660 --> 02:41.300 So depending on the user query, the orchestrator first examines the initial request, dynamically identifies 02:41.340 --> 02:48.900 necessary subtasks such as designing the user interface, and in the case of the e-commerce site, sets 02:48.940 --> 02:52.900 up payment processing and develops inventory management.
  • 02:53.420 --> 02:59.900 When building a corporate website, the steps include creating a blog and an About Us page.
  • 03:00.380 --> 03:08.820 Each identified subtask is then delegated to specialized worker who solve their assigned tasks independently.
  • 03:09.540 --> 03:17.420 Finally, the results are sent to a synthesizer LM, which integrates them into a cohesive and comprehensive 03:17.420 --> 03:18.180 solution.

Lesson 69: Evaluator-optimizer

00:05.720 --> 00:13.320 Another intriguing workflow we'll explore is the Evaluator Optimizer pattern, which consists of two 00:13.360 --> 00:14.600 core components. 00:15.240 --> 00:23.320 On one side is the generator LM responsible for producing an initial solution based on the user's query.

Core Concept

Another intriguing workflow we'll explore is the Evaluator Optimizer pattern, which consists of two core components. On one side is the generator LM responsible for producing an initial solution based on the user's query. On the other side is the evaluator LM, which critically assesses the generator's output, highlighting its strengths, weaknesses, and opportunities for improvement.

Key Points

  • The evaluator then communicates its constructive feedback to the generator LM, prompting it to revise and refine the original solution.
  • Through this iterative feedback loop, the generator progressively enhances the quality of its output.
  • After several iterations of evaluation and refinement, the evaluator eventually recognizes when the solution meets the desired standards and approves it as an outcome.
  • This approach is suitable for scenarios that demand precision and continuous improvement.
  • One example of such a task can be content creation.
  • Imagine a scenario where you want to apply this workflow to generate social media content.
  • You want the final output to be in sync with your company's brand guidelines, social media best practices, marketing strategy, and ethical guidelines.
  • Therefore, the final output will be evaluated based on several nuanced criteria.
💡 From the Lecture
01:18.150 --> 01:23.950 Imagine a scenario where you want to apply this workflow to generate social media content.
Key Takeaways
  • 01:53.870 --> 01:57.470 After all, humans work in a very similar way, don't we?
  • 01:58.110 --> 02:02.550 When we work on a task, we don't submit our first draft instantly.
  • 02:02.950 --> 02:08.910 Instead, we review it a few times to ensure it meets the requirements of our organization set.
  • 02:09.470 --> 02:17.310 Similarly, the Evaluator Optimizer workflow uses an iterative refinement process to polish the system's 02:17.310 --> 02:18.710 final output.

Lesson 71: When to Use a Single Agent Architecture

00:05.560 --> 00:12.200 In the following few lessons, we'll explore several examples of single agent architectures, including 00:12.200 --> 00:15.440 reflection, react, and reflection. 00:16.160 --> 00:23.840 A typical pattern you'll notice is that single agents often include planning and self-correction capabilities.

Core Concept

In the following few lessons, we'll explore several examples of single agent architectures, including reflection, react, and reflection. A typical pattern you'll notice is that single agents often include planning and self-correction capabilities. Without these mechanisms, they would risk entering an infinite loop of execution.

Key Points

  • Planning is a necessary step in the reasoning process, where the agent reflects on how to solve the problem at hand in an optimal way.
  • This occurs before any concrete actions are carried out.
  • By forming a plan, the agent can break down the task into manageable steps, evaluate different options, and select the most promising course of action.
  • Another critical aspect of single agent systems is their self-correction ability.
  • As the agent starts acting, it needs a mechanism that allows it to monitor its performance and reflect on intermediate outcomes.
  • This allows the agent to reassess and adjust its actions if things aren't going as planned.
  • In the upcoming lessons, you'll see how the cycle of planning, acting, reevaluating and correcting lies at the heart of most single agent systems.

Lesson 72: Reflection

Core Concept

In this lesson, we want to consider a single agent architecture called reflection. Reflection basically involves an agent that receives a user request, provides an initial response, and then reflects on the response to determine whether it meets the required quality. If the response needs further refinement, the agent revises it before delivering the final output to the user.

Key Points

  • This process can be repeated as many times as necessary before the system concludes that it has produced satisfactory output.
  • Now you might ask, hey, didn't we just study this type of architecture?
  • Just a few lessons ago in the Agentic Workflow Patterns section?
  • And you'd be absolutely right to point that out.
  • The idea behind reflection is identical to the one described in the Evaluator Optimizer workflow structure.
  • The main difference evaluator optimizer is an agentic workflow featuring two specialized LM roles, a generator and an evaluator.
  • In this section of the course, however, we're focusing on single agent architectures.
  • Therefore, we can expect that the reflection single agent structure will use this pattern, but in a self-contained mechanism within one agent, the same agent acts, reviews its actions and then acts again.

  • 02:36.970 --> 02:43.970 Rather than settling for the first response it generates, the agent pauses to evaluate and improve, 02:44.130 --> 02:47.890 resulting in a more thoughtful and polished result.
