Lesson 73: ReAct (Think-Do)

00:05.480 --> 00:06.320 All right. 00:06.320 --> 00:07.640 We're doing great. 00:08.120 --> 00:15.120 The first type of single agent architecture we considered was reflection, which focused on evaluating 00:15.120 --> 00:19.200 whether the agent's output met the desired quality standards.

Core Concept

We're doing great. The first type of single agent architecture we considered was reflection, which focused on evaluating whether the agent's output met the desired quality standards. Please notice that in the reflection architecture, the system refrains from producing any external output or acting until it determines, through internal reasoning, that its result is satisfactory.

Key Points

  • The next key framework we'll examine is react, a term that derived from the words reason and act.
  • In this type of system, the agent first engages in reasoning before taking any action.
  • The agent observes the result of its actions and considers the next optimal action.
  • The key difference from the reflection pattern is that this agent operates with a proactive, can do mentality.
  • Ready to act and learn from the consequences of its actions.
  • This type of proactive behavior is optimal when we want to assign the agent tasks that require several intermediate steps.
  • The agent's reasoning capabilities enable it to handle tasks that cannot be fully resolved through internal reflection alone.
  • Instead of trying to plan everything perfectly beforehand, react encourages the agent to take action, learn from the outcome, and adjust accordingly.
💡 From the Lecture
01:00.640 --> 01:07.760 The key difference from the reflection pattern is that this agent operates with a proactive, can do 01:07.800 --> 01:08.640 mentality.
💡 From the Lecture
01:43.600 --> 01:49.720 For instance, consider a react agent attempting to schedule a meeting with a client.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:41.810 --> 02:44.050 Reasoning and acting.
  • 02:44.770 --> 02:51.450 Unlike reflection, where the agent remains in its own internal loop until it's satisfied with the result, 02:51.730 --> 03:00.570 react emphasizes thinking through action, breaking a complex problem into smaller steps and learning 03:00.570 --> 03:01.490 from each one.
  • 03:01.970 --> 03:09.570 A significant limitation of react is that the model sometimes repetitively generates the same thoughts 03:09.570 --> 03:15.850 and actions, failing to create new ones, which could result in stagnation loops.
  • 03:16.170 --> 03:19.730 Human intervention is necessary when this occurs.

Lesson 74: Reflexion

00:05.720 --> 00:10.800 The next single agent design pattern we'll explore is reflection. 00:11.400 --> 00:15.920 It closely resembles react, but with one key distinction. 00:17.160 --> 00:23.800 With reflection, an agent is assigned a specific task and then reasons through the problem in an effort 00:23.800 --> 00:24.600 to solve it.

Core Concept

The next single agent design pattern we'll explore is reflection. It closely resembles react, but with one key distinction. With reflection, an agent is assigned a specific task and then reasons through the problem in an effort to solve it.

Key Points

  • Reflection either resolves the problem successfully or recognizes its own failure.
  • In both cases, the agent records a self-reflection summary and stores it permanently.
  • As a result, the experience from this episode becomes part of the agent's knowledge, influencing all future interactions.
  • The key feature of this architecture is its memory and the learning capabilities that stem from it.
  • This is what allows the agent to learn from mistakes and improve over time.
  • And that's the main difference between react and reflection.
  • With react, we have an AI agent which does not retain knowledge over different episodes.
  • It reasons, takes actions and can reflect within a single task.
💡 From the Lecture
00:48.440 --> 00:54.680 The key feature of this architecture is its memory and the learning capabilities that stem from it.
Key Takeaways
  • 01:49.770 --> 01:56.250 As a result of these capabilities, reflection agents tend to have improved success rates compared to 01:56.290 --> 01:57.490 react agents.
  • 01:58.090 --> 02:05.170 The primary limitation of reflection agents, however, is the token limit of the language model used.
  • 02:05.690 --> 02:12.890 Because reflection agents can store vast amounts of information in their long term memory, it can sometimes 02:12.930 --> 02:20.450 be challenging to determine which past reflections are most relevant to retrieve and apply to a new 02:20.450 --> 02:21.130 task.
  • 02:21.570 --> 02:29.010 This introduces the need for effective memory management and retrieval strategies, such as ranking 02:29.010 --> 02:35.810 past reflections by similarity to the current task or summarizing long term memory.

Lesson 78: Plan and Solve

00:06.520 --> 00:07.240 Excellent. 00:07.560 --> 00:11.320 Plan and solve is the first planning pattern we'll cover. 00:12.040 --> 00:15.680 As the name suggests, it runs in two stages. 00:16.160 --> 00:23.960 First, the agent plans by assessing the task at hand, identifying the available resources, and considering 00:23.960 --> 00:25.680 any relevant constraints.

Core Concept

Okay. Excellent. Plan and solve is the first planning pattern we'll cover.

Key Points

  • As the name suggests, it runs in two stages.
  • First, the agent plans by assessing the task at hand, identifying the available resources, and considering any relevant constraints.
  • Next, the agent moves on to selecting the right tools for the job and breaking the work into a precise sequence of steps.
  • In the second stage, the agent solves the task by executing the planned steps.
  • What's characteristic of the plan and solve pattern is that in the second stage, the system can replan and refine its initial strategy that occurs when a step fails, or when it becomes clear that the original plan needs adjustment.
  • Ideally, at each step, your system should include mechanisms for output verification, ensuring that the result of the current step meets the requirements of the next step.
  • If it doesn't, the agent replans and updates the task list as shown in the visualization.
  • Once all steps pass verification, the result is returned to the user.
Key Takeaways
  • 01:00.320 --> 01:07.000 Ideally, at each step, your system should include mechanisms for output verification, ensuring that 01:07.000 --> 01:11.560 the result of the current step meets the requirements of the next step.
  • 01:12.120 --> 01:18.960 If it doesn't, the agent replans and updates the task list as shown in the visualization.
  • 01:19.400 --> 01:24.600 Once all steps pass verification, the result is returned to the user.
  • 01:25.200 --> 01:31.600 If we were to summarize the plan and solve pattern in just a few words, they would be plan the route, 01:32.080 --> 01:35.480 execute and verify if needed.

Lesson 79: ReWOO

00:05.560 --> 00:12.200 Riwu is another vital planning pattern, short for reasoning without observation. 00:12.640 --> 00:18.280 The underlying logic is quite similar to the plan and solve approach we just discussed.

Core Concept

Riwu is another vital planning pattern, short for reasoning without observation. The underlying logic is quite similar to the plan and solve approach we just discussed. Riwu is an agent architecture that separates reasoning managed by a planner from task execution, managed by a worker, and concludes with a solver that synthesizes the final output.

Key Points

  • This separation of roles enables more efficient token usage.
  • A noticeable difference with respect to plan and solve is that riwu does not allow for reassessments and replanning after every action has been taken.
  • The entire plan is created beforehand and remains fixed until all tasks in the task list are completed.
  • There won't be any changes to the plan based on subsequent observations, or if the agent fails to execute intermediate steps that are part of the initial plan.
  • Let's consider a personal assistant tasked with scheduling a meeting with Riwu.
  • The agent first carefully plans the entire sequence of steps from start to finish before taking any action.
  • It collects evidence after planning, but doesn't replan accordingly, meaning it won't adapt its actions based on intermediate tool outputs.
  • Following this comprehensive planning phase, the plan is executed without deviation.
💡 From the Lecture
01:10.110 --> 01:16.110 Let's consider a personal assistant tasked with scheduling a meeting with Riwu.
💡 From the Lecture
02:26.250 --> 02:33.890 Of course, both frameworks have their pros and cons and are preferable in different AI agent use cases 02:34.410 --> 02:36.610 compared to the plan and solve pattern.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:47.490 --> 02:53.130 We have all the relevant information up front and the cost of replanting is high.
  • 02:53.730 --> 03:02.170 Therefore, with Riwu, we need to lock in a perfect plan and follow it without deviation or mid-course 03:02.170 --> 03:03.050 corrections.
  • 03:03.570 --> 03:08.690 Plan and solve, on the other hand, is better suited for situations where conditions change.
  • 03:08.890 --> 03:15.050 Intermediate results uncover new requirements, and adaptability is critical.

Lesson 80: Tree of Thought

00:05.840 --> 00:13.480 The next planning pattern we'll consider is called Tree of Thought tot not to be mistaken for chain 00:13.520 --> 00:17.640 of thought cot, which represents a different concept.

Core Concept

The next planning pattern we'll consider is called Tree of Thought tot not to be mistaken for chain of thought cot, which represents a different concept. Tree of thought is a unique agent architecture that merges planning with exploratory search to enhance problem solving capability, meaning that the AI system doesn't create a single plan of action it plans for multiple future states, compares them, and selects the best one of them. The focus of this system is to perform complex reasoning by considering multiple solution strategies.

Key Points

  • It's best employed in situations where you must solve a complex problem, such as a difficult math problem, or comparing several alternative solutions.
  • In general, the tree of thought framework is meant for situations when the solution space is ample and branching exploration can reveal better strategies.
  • Tree of thought can identify the optimal solution by evaluating multiple potential paths, thereby minimizing the risk of becoming trapped on a single flawed line of reasoning.
  • On the negative side, tree of thought is significantly more expensive in terms of token usage and can be slower due to the exploration of many branches.
Key Takeaways
  • 01:00.440 --> 01:06.520 In general, the tree of thought framework is meant for situations when the solution space is ample 01:06.520 --> 01:10.640 and branching exploration can reveal better strategies.
  • 01:11.280 --> 01:18.760 Tree of thought can identify the optimal solution by evaluating multiple potential paths, thereby minimizing 01:18.760 --> 01:23.600 the risk of becoming trapped on a single flawed line of reasoning.
  • 01:23.960 --> 01:30.840 On the negative side, tree of thought is significantly more expensive in terms of token usage and can 01:30.840 --> 01:34.840 be slower due to the exploration of many branches.
  • 01:35.240 --> 01:39.160 It's far from ideal for simple tasks.

Lesson 82: When to Use Single vs. Multi-agent Systems

00:05.840 --> 00:14.160 Deciding between a single agent or multi-agent setup comes down to what best fits your current use case. 00:14.720 --> 00:21.920 In certain cases, the simplicity of a single agent structure is more effective, especially when managing 00:21.920 --> 00:27.520 well-defined processes that don't demand input from multiple specialists.

Core Concept

Deciding between a single agent or multi-agent setup comes down to what best fits your current use case. In certain cases, the simplicity of a single agent structure is more effective, especially when managing well-defined processes that don't demand input from multiple specialists. Think of it like this.

Key Points

  • In a company, a social media manager can independently create and publish an Instagram post.
  • But launching an omnichannel marketing campaign is an entirely different matter, typically involving collaboration among a copywriter, graphic designer, ads specialist and marketing manager.
  • When a social media manager independently creates and publishes an Instagram post, the task is simple enough for one skilled individual to handle.
  • In contrast, launching an omnichannel marketing campaign introduces far more complexity, requiring a team of specialists whose combined expertise can deliver a high quality result.
  • Another advantage of single agents is that they avoid some of the pitfalls that arise in multi-agent setups when multiple agents collaborate.
  • There's a risk that they might distract one another.
  • Duplicate efforts on the same activity or provide poor feedback to each other's work.
  • The main challenge AI engineers must address when working with a single agent is preventing it from getting stuck in an endless execution loop.
💡 From the Lecture
00:05.840 --> 00:14.160 Deciding between a single agent or multi-agent setup comes down to what best fits your current use case.
💡 From the Lecture
00:28.480 --> 00:29.600 Think of it like this.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:53.810 --> 03:01.570 Research also shows that multi-agent systems tend to perform better in zero shot scenarios, when no 03:01.570 --> 03:04.250 examples are provided in the system prompt.
  • 03:04.530 --> 03:05.330 The takeaway.
  • 03:05.850 --> 03:11.330 Choosing between single and multi-agent designs goes beyond reasoning capabilities.
  • 03:11.450 --> 03:18.850 It's about the broader context, the tasks, nature, time constraints, and available resources.

Lesson 83: Vertical vs Horizontal Architectures

00:05.640 --> 00:08.400 When considering multi-agent systems. 00:08.440 --> 00:14.080 A key architecture distinction lies between vertical and horizontal designs. 00:14.600 --> 00:21.080 In a vertical architecture, a single leader directs the group, with all other agents reporting directly 00:21.080 --> 00:22.160 to that leader.

Core Concept

When considering multi-agent systems. A key architecture distinction lies between vertical and horizontal designs. In a vertical architecture, a single leader directs the group, with all other agents reporting directly to that leader.

Key Points

  • In some cases, agents will talk exclusively with their manager.
  • In other instances, they will communicate with each other in a shared conversation, but the lead will assign tasks and approve the outputs of individual agents.
  • Vertical architecture typically has lower latency for decision making because there's a clear leader assigning tasks and approving outputs.
  • Communication flows in a defined path so you avoid the overhead of full group discussions.
  • The key characteristics of the vertical architecture choice include a clear division of labor, and a single figure responsible for assigning work to individual agents.
  • A horizontal architecture, by contrast, features a flat structure where all agents are equal and communicate through a shared thread.
  • Each agent can assess and read every message, ensuring complete and mutual awareness.
  • Delegation occurs through a volunteering mechanism where agents volunteer to complete tasks.
💡 From the Lecture
00:57.480 --> 01:03.800 The key characteristics of the vertical architecture choice include a clear division of labor, and 01:03.800 --> 01:08.760 a single figure responsible for assigning work to individual agents.
💡 From the Lecture
02:18.840 --> 02:25.560 The key is to align the architecture with the tasks requirements, achieving the best balance between 02:25.560 --> 02:28.280 efficiency and output quality.
Key Takeaways
  • 01:54.240 --> 02:01.120 In summary, the choice between a vertical or horizontal multi-agent architecture ultimately depends 02:01.120 --> 02:03.120 on your specific objectives.
  • 02:03.600 --> 02:10.120 A vertical setup provides structure and ensures clear guidance throughout the entire process.
  • 02:10.640 --> 02:18.280 A horizontal setup promotes openness, enabling agents to collaborate equally and exchange ideas freely.
  • 02:18.840 --> 02:25.560 The key is to align the architecture with the tasks requirements, achieving the best balance between 02:25.560 --> 02:28.280 efficiency and output quality.

Lesson 84: Challenges with Group Conversations

00:05.680 --> 00:11.240 A single agent stays focused without being distracted by external input. 00:11.760 --> 00:18.200 On the contrary, it remains focused, completing the task using its own abilities and the available 00:18.200 --> 00:19.120 information.

Core Concept

A single agent stays focused without being distracted by external input. On the contrary, it remains focused, completing the task using its own abilities and the available information. That focus is a considerable advantage over multi-agent architectures, which often face challenges with group conversation and information sharing in a horizontal architecture.

Key Points

  • Agents often end up wasting time on unnecessary chatter and pleasantries when multiple agents read the same thread.
  • It can result in inefficient resource use and higher latency.
  • Agents might waste time on casual exchanges like how are you?
  • Instead of focusing on advancing the task.
  • To address this issue, AI engineers use robust, prompt engineering that forbids distractions and unnecessary conversations that don't contribute to the task at hand.
  • In a vertical architecture, the risk of distractions is much lower since agents communicate directly with the lead agent.
  • But since agents don't communicate directly with one another, there may be instances where subordinate agents lack the information needed to perform their tasks effectively.
  • This can be problematic and could lead to confusion and even hallucination in some instances.
Key Takeaways
  • 01:17.360 --> 01:24.480 But since agents don't communicate directly with one another, there may be instances where subordinate 01:24.480 --> 01:29.480 agents lack the information needed to perform their tasks effectively.
  • 01:29.840 --> 01:37.120 This can be problematic and could lead to confusion and even hallucination in some instances.
  • 01:37.760 --> 01:45.360 The solution is to define access permissions in the system prompt, enabling subordinate agents to receive 01:45.360 --> 01:46.920 the necessary information.
  • 01:47.440 --> 01:53.920 These are two considerations to keep in mind when working with multi-agent architectures, whether in 01:53.920 --> 01:56.760 a horizontal or vertical setup.

  • We had an LM acting as a router, deciding which agents should handle the user query.
  • The supervisor architecture is quite similar, featuring a supervisor agent who coordinates the agents.
  • It's a classic example of top down control, with the supervisor acting as the central decision maker.
  • The key difference between the supervisor architecture and the routing workflow is that supervisor is a more intelligent solution.
  • It doesn't just assign tasks, it takes on a broader managerial boss role.
  • Yes, it delegates tasks, but the supervisor also reviews outputs, provides feedback to the other agents, and can break larger tasks into smaller subtasks.
  • Let's consider a customer support scenario as an example.

Lesson 86: Hierarchical Teams

00:05.680 --> 00:06.360 All right. 00:06.720 --> 00:13.320 We just explored the supervisor architecture, a structure where a single agent acts as the supervisor, 00:13.480 --> 00:20.400 managing several subordinate agents, assigning tasks, offering feedback, and reviewing their output.

Core Concept

We just explored the supervisor architecture, a structure where a single agent acts as the supervisor, managing several subordinate agents, assigning tasks, offering feedback, and reviewing their output. A real life analogy would be a small firm where a manager supervises a team of employees. In this type of business, there's limited specialization so the manager can effectively oversee the work of 4 or 5 employees, sometimes even as many as 7 or 8.

Key Points

  • But as the business continues to grow, it eventually reaches a point where a new organizational structure is needed to manage operations effectively.
  • A single manager cannot effectively supervise 20 or 30 people.
  • The workload becomes unmanageable, communication deteriorates, and quality control begins to decline.
  • At that stage, the business usually evolves into a more layered structure where the original manager delegates oversight to other managers.
  • This creates a hierarchical chain of command.
  • Likewise, when handling tasks that require coordinating many agents, a single agent may not be capable of effectively managing them all.
  • Moreover, it could be beneficial if manager agents are also specialized in the task the team has been assigned.
  • Consider a hierarchical team of agents that can create a marketing campaign from scratch.
💡 From the Lecture
01:37.530 --> 01:43.890 Consider a hierarchical team of agents that can create a marketing campaign from scratch.
💡 From the Lecture
01:44.450 --> 01:48.930 We might, for example, have a team of agents specializing in copywriting.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:08.090 --> 02:14.850 The managers would then report to a supervising manager who oversees the entire operation, maintaining 02:14.850 --> 02:21.210 the big picture perspective, coordinating the efforts of all specialized teams, and ensuring that 02:21.210 --> 02:24.890 everything aligns with the campaign's overall goals.
  • 02:25.530 --> 02:32.250 In other words, while each specialized manager focuses on excellence within their own domain, the 02:32.250 --> 02:41.130 supervisor manager ensures coordination across domains, resolves conflicts between teams, and manages 02:41.130 --> 02:44.850 timelines and priorities at the project level.
  • 02:45.730 --> 02:52.170 The hierarchical team architecture is suitable for complex and comprehensive use cases.
  • 02:52.530 --> 02:59.970 This structure improves scalability, communication and quality control, but it also demands careful 02:59.970 --> 03:07.290 planning to prevent bottlenecks at the top and ensure that accurate information flows smoothly through 03:07.330 --> 03:08.250 each layer.

Lesson 87: Dynamic Teams

00:05.520 --> 00:13.640 Next, we'll consider dynamic teams a flexible and adaptive pattern where teams are assembled, disassembled, 00:13.640 --> 00:15.800 and reconfigured as needed. 00:16.440 --> 00:23.160 The dynamic reassignment feature of this architecture is useful in situations where agents need to be 00:23.200 --> 00:28.560 added or removed from the system, depending on current needs and workload.

Core Concept

Next, we'll consider dynamic teams a flexible and adaptive pattern where teams are assembled, disassembled, and reconfigured as needed. The dynamic reassignment feature of this architecture is useful in situations where agents need to be added or removed from the system, depending on current needs and workload. We should remember that even though the composition of dynamic teams changes, they continue to have an authority layer that assigns tasks.

Key Points

  • For this reason, dynamic teams are a vertical type of architecture.
  • Some might argue that dynamic teams don't follow a strictly vertical hierarchy, especially when teams are disbanded and all agents return to a shared pool without fixed reporting lines.
  • At that point, the structure becomes more horizontal, wouldn't you say?
  • For a short while, agents become peers and interact as equals.
  • But soon after, when a new team configuration is formed, the vertical layer of authority naturally reemerges.
  • Therefore, since dynamic teams operate within a vertical structure most of the time, particularly during their most productive phases, we can also classify this type of architecture as vertical.
💡 From the Lecture
00:29.080 --> 00:34.880 We should remember that even though the composition of dynamic teams changes, they continue to have 00:34.880 --> 00:37.680 an authority layer that assigns tasks.
Key Takeaways

Lesson 89: Agents and Asyncronous Task Execution

00:05.640 --> 00:11.680 What's the most effective way to speed up a task that involves a lot of hands on work? 00:12.280 --> 00:12.960 Simple. 00:13.280 --> 00:16.400 Get more people working on it in parallel.

Core Concept

What's the most effective way to speed up a task that involves a lot of hands on work? Simple. Get more people working on it in parallel.

Key Points

  • In this lesson, we'll use this idea to explore asynchronous task execution and highlight the key difference between single and multi-agent systems.
  • In many real world tasks, if one person handles everything sequentially, the overall pace is limited by that individual's speed.
  • But if you can split up the work into several parts and involve multiple people working on them simultaneously, you can often finish much faster.
  • Synchronous execution means an agent waits for one task to finish before starting the next.
  • Asynchronous execution allows tasks to run in parallel without blocking one another if they don't rely on each other's results.
  • Imagine a baker preparing ten cakes alone.
  • They start by measuring ingredients, mixing the batter, baking and decorating.
  • Completing each step for cake number one before moving on to cake number two.
💡 From the Lecture
00:17.080 --> 00:25.040 In this lesson, we'll use this idea to explore asynchronous task execution and highlight the key difference 00:25.040 --> 00:28.440 between single and multi-agent systems.
💡 From the Lecture
00:29.160 --> 00:36.480 In many real world tasks, if one person handles everything sequentially, the overall pace is limited 00:36.480 --> 00:38.400 by that individual's speed.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:45.190 --> 02:52.750 In multi-agent setups, different agents often handle separate subtasks independently, with a coordinator 02:52.750 --> 02:54.670 agent combining their outputs.
  • 02:54.910 --> 03:02.030 Naturally, the advantage of asynchronous execution with multiple agents is its ability to reduce latency.
  • 03:02.430 --> 03:09.430 Moreover, this approach enables scalability because this type of structure prepares the AI agent system 03:09.590 --> 03:11.430 for larger workloads.
  • 03:11.950 --> 03:18.630 We should remember, however, that not all tasks can benefit from async execution if the intermediate 03:18.630 --> 03:26.150 steps needed to solve the task at hand require results that depend on the previous step, we cannot 03:26.150 --> 03:28.790 rely on asynchronous execution.

Lesson 90: Performance Metrics - Latency and Cost

00:05.640 --> 00:08.520 When agents are deployed in a live environment. 00:08.520 --> 00:14.480 Two key questions to ask are one how fast is the solution we've launched? 00:14.480 --> 00:18.280 And two how much does it cost to operate?

Core Concept

When agents are deployed in a live environment. Two key questions to ask are one how fast is the solution we've launched? And two how much does it cost to operate?

Key Points

  • Ideally, before going live, we've confirmed that the agent can solve the intended problem.
  • Now it's time to assess whether it can do so efficiently.
  • Staying within the performance and budget constraints of a real world environment, latency can be divided into two main components model interference latency and orchestration.
  • Model interference depends on the type of model you select for your agent system.
  • Generally, larger models exhibit higher latency, and the prompt length you send to the model also plays a significant role.
  • For example, a GPT five call with a long chain of thought may take several seconds, while a GPT four turbo call on a short prompt may return in under a second beyond the model's response time.
  • These delays can arise from processes like chaining prompts, waiting for parallel tasks to complete, performing memory lookups from a vector database, calling external APIs or tools, or coordinating multiple agents.
  • In practice, orchestration overhead can be just as significant as model response time, sometimes even larger, especially in multi-agent systems.
💡 From the Lecture
00:29.040 --> 00:36.200 Staying within the performance and budget constraints of a real world environment, latency can be divided 00:36.200 --> 00:41.840 into two main components model interference latency and orchestration.
💡 From the Lecture
00:57.120 --> 01:05.960 For example, a GPT five call with a long chain of thought may take several seconds, while a GPT four 01:06.000 --> 01:13.680 turbo call on a short prompt may return in under a second beyond the model's response time.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:56.470 --> 03:03.070 These considerations determine the runtime efficiency of the agent system we've designed today.
  • 03:03.070 --> 03:09.350 It takes significant experience and AI engineering effort to design a truly optimized system.
  • 03:09.870 --> 03:17.070 AI engineers continually evaluate latency cost trade offs across different scenarios to determine the 03:17.070 --> 03:19.110 most effective course of action.
  • 03:19.470 --> 03:26.310 The key takeaway is that building effective agents isn't just about solving the problem, it's about 03:26.310 --> 03:28.030 doing it efficiently.

Lesson 91: Error Handling and Recovery

00:05.440 --> 00:12.240 The latency and cost optimization performance metrics we examined in the previous lesson are intended 00:12.240 --> 00:16.280 for situations where the agent system works as intended.

Core Concept

The latency and cost optimization performance metrics we examined in the previous lesson are intended for situations where the agent system works as intended. This means the agent can accomplish its intended goals while striving to achieve optimal performance. But sometimes things don't go as planned.

Key Points

  • That's when error handling and recovery matter most.
  • To accomplish their goals, agents depend on several interconnected components.
  • They draw reasoning from an Lem, connect to external tools through APIs, and in some cases receive input from other agents.
  • So naturally, the more sophisticated a structure, the higher the chances of failures.
  • It may not happen all the time, but it does occur at least occasionally.
  • LMS may go offline for maintenance or produce unexpected outputs, while external tools can experience temporary outages or return incomplete data.
  • External agents can miscommunicate and many other issues can arise along the way.
  • This is why robust error handling and recovery mechanisms are essential parts of any production ready agent architecture.
💡 From the Lecture
00:16.800 --> 00:23.440 This means the agent can accomplish its intended goals while striving to achieve optimal performance.
💡 From the Lecture
01:36.330 --> 01:45.690 For instance, you could implement retry logic for failed LM calls or even route requests to an alternative 01:45.730 --> 01:46.330 LM.
Key Takeaways
  • 01:51.810 --> 01:58.770 Similar procedures can be created for other parts of the system, such as APIs and agent to agent communication.
  • 01:59.330 --> 02:07.250 Ultimately, the goal isn't to eliminate every error that's unrealistic, but to ensure the system can 02:07.250 --> 02:13.810 fail gracefully and continue progressing towards its objectives without a complete breakdown.
  • 02:14.450 --> 02:21.330 We want to ensure that the end user's experience remains smooth and uninterrupted, even when specific 02:21.330 --> 02:25.770 components are unavailable or performing below optimal levels.
  • 02:26.450 --> 02:34.170 Designing reliable error handling and recovery mechanisms is one of the most complex and demanding challenges 02:34.170 --> 02:40.090 in AI engineering, requiring substantial effort in every project you undertake.

00:05.680 --> 00:11.240 For most real world applications you'll work on, you'll quickly realize the importance of building 00:11.240 --> 00:15.480 an AI driven system that can remember past interactions.

Core Concept

For most real world applications you'll work on, you'll quickly realize the importance of building an AI driven system that can remember past interactions. In other words, you'll need to add a memory component to your agents by remembering and reusing information over time. We enable agents to learn from past interactions.

Key Points

  • Think of it like this without memory, agents are like goldfish, able to complete a task but unable to retain any insights or lessons afterward.
  • That's acceptable for simple tools such as a weighing scale, but by incorporating memory into the system, it can remember past performance and use that knowledge to improve future outcomes.
  • That's what makes Netflix's and YouTube's recommendation engines more accurate the longer you use them.
  • The system doesn't just suggest random items each time it keeps track of your past preferences, adapts to your choices, and refines its predictions.
  • Memory is what makes specific AI agent systems sophisticated as it enables learning.
  • In this section of the course, we'll cover two key types of memory.
  • Short term context buffer, the agent's temporary memory that records recent events, and vector store rag, a more advanced technique that embeds interactions as vectors and stores them in a searchable database.
  • Finally, we'll explore entity level memory, a specialized form of memory designed to retain details about specific entities such as individuals or organizations.

Lesson 93: Short-term Context Buffer

00:05.600 --> 00:11.960 The most basic type of memory we can give an AI agent is known as a short term context buffer. 00:12.480 --> 00:18.480 This enables the AI agent to retain and reference a limited number of recent interactions.

Core Concept

The most basic type of memory we can give an AI agent is known as a short term context buffer. This enables the AI agent to retain and reference a limited number of recent interactions. Imagine you've built a chatbot that's powered by one of OpenAI's GPT models.

Key Points

  • Interestingly, the OpenAI API doesn't include built in memory by default.
  • Each API call is stateless and forgets prior interactions unless you explicitly provide the previous context in your request.
  • If you were to design a short term memory mechanism, you'd essentially decide to retain the last, let's say, ten messages and include them again with each new request.
  • In this setup, the agent remembers only the ten most recent messages.
  • Once the conversation goes beyond that limit, it forgets earlier exchanges.
  • That's one of the key limitations of short term context memory.
  • Once the buffer overflows, the forgotten content is lost for good.
  • The agent can access only what fits within its defined context window.
💡 From the Lecture
00:18.800 --> 00:24.320 Imagine you've built a chatbot that's powered by one of OpenAI's GPT models.

Key Takeaways
  • 02:28.460 --> 02:35.740 Because the agent only retains limited information, it can respond quickly and handle each conversation 02:35.740 --> 02:37.980 with a relatively clear mind.
  • 02:38.380 --> 02:45.460 The limitation is obvious, right when you need more context and longer term memory.
  • 02:45.780 --> 02:47.900 This approach is not sufficient.
  • 02:48.340 --> 02:55.580 That's why more advanced methods like vector stores and entity level memory are needed for long term 02:55.580 --> 02:56.500 context.

Lesson 94: Vector store RAG

00:05.760 --> 00:12.640 The key drawback of short term memory is that it doesn't allow our agent to store a significant number 00:12.640 --> 00:14.280 of past interactions. 00:15.280 --> 00:23.040 Ideally, the agent should be capable of continuing a conversation exactly where it left off, drawing 00:23.040 --> 00:29.560 on a rich store of knowledge to make the interaction feel more natural and contextually relevant.

Core Concept

The key drawback of short term memory is that it doesn't allow our agent to store a significant number of past interactions. Ideally, the agent should be capable of continuing a conversation exactly where it left off, drawing on a rich store of knowledge to make the interaction feel more natural and contextually relevant. Someone with a good memory can recall past experiences and respond to questions about things they learned long ago.

Key Points

  • Similarly, for an agent to appear truly intelligent, it must be able to recall past interactions and use that knowledge to deliver more accurate and insightful responses.
  • Rather than starting from scratch each time, it should build on what has already been discussed.
  • Just as humans rely on memory to keep conversations coherent and meaningful, we need a method that makes this possible.
  • And that's where Vector Store Rag comes in.
  • You may already know this, but Rag stands for retrieval Augmented Generation.
  • Put simply, it's a technique that retrieves relevant information from existing knowledge sources and feeds it to an LLM, helping the model to generate more accurate and insightful responses.
  • Think of a company developing a chatbot for internal use.
  • Its purpose is to help employees get answers to questions about company policies, privacy guidelines, and HR procedures.
💡 From the Lecture
00:05.760 --> 00:12.640 The key drawback of short term memory is that it doesn't allow our agent to store a significant number 00:12.640 --> 00:14.280 of past interactions.

02:11.050 --> 02:19.010 This is done by converting the information into vectors, essentially translating text into numerical 02:19.010 --> 02:23.330 representations that the model can understand and work with.
Key Takeaways
  • 03:29.250 --> 03:35.810 Moreover, searching through thousands of pages can add significant latency to your project in some 03:35.810 --> 03:36.690 instances.
  • 03:37.050 --> 03:44.690 Rag represents a significant step toward building agents that can genuinely remember and apply knowledge 03:44.690 --> 03:46.570 in a way that feels intelligent.

Lesson 95: Entity-level Memory

00:05.560 --> 00:09.680 The third type of memory we'll cover is entity level memory. 00:10.280 --> 00:17.680 This type of memory focuses on retaining information about specific entities such as people, companies, 00:17.680 --> 00:18.680 or products.

Core Concept

The third type of memory we'll cover is entity level memory. This type of memory focuses on retaining information about specific entities such as people, companies, or products. For example, imagine a chatbot installed as an app on your phone.

Key Points

  • Entity level memory is designed to learn about you, your preferences, habits, and past interactions, allowing it to personalize responses and adapt over time.
  • Each time you add information about yourself in your conversations with the chatbot, the agent will add this information to its knowledge repository.
  • So the next time you interact with it, the agent will consider the information it previously stored before generating a response.
  • This allows the agent to provide much more thoughtful responses.
  • Let's say you're chatting with a bot that uses entity level memory, and you've mentioned that you live in Italy.
  • The next time you ask the agent about the weather, it will already know to show the temperature in Celsius.
  • This type of memory is focused on providing a personalized experience over time.
  • It can be beneficial in a business context when the industry and product you work on remain stable.

Lesson 97: Self-reflection

00:05.400 --> 00:12.880 Every problem is solved through a sequence of small reasoning steps, each comparable to a single move 00:12.880 --> 00:14.920 in the overall thinking process. 00:17.000 --> 00:22.840 On Monday morning, I need to decide whether to commute to the office by car or by bicycle.

Core Concept

Every problem is solved through a sequence of small reasoning steps, each comparable to a single move in the overall thinking process. On Monday morning, I need to decide whether to commute to the office by car or by bicycle. There are several factors I'll take into account one.

Key Points

  • I'll remember that Mondays usually have heavy traffic.
  • Two next, I'll compare the car and the bicycle, concluding that traffic would delay me by about 15 minutes.
  • If I choose to drive three, then comes calculation.
  • I'll estimate the time needed to park the car near the office versus the time required to lock up the bike.
  • In this case, the bike is the faster option once again, so I'll go ahead and eliminate the car as an option.
  • I'll also recall that if I take the bicycle, I won't be able to go to the gym afterward.
  • See how many small intermediate reasoning steps I used for this decision.
  • The self-reflection planning method enables agents to determine the most effective way to solve complex problems independently.
💡 From the Lecture
00:30.600 --> 00:34.480 I'll remember that Mondays usually have heavy traffic.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:14.630 --> 02:22.270 But by incorporating comparison, calculation, elimination, and an additional recall step, I arrived 02:22.270 --> 02:25.150 at a more well-considered conclusion.
  • 02:25.590 --> 02:29.590 That's precisely how self-discovery works in Llms.
  • 02:29.910 --> 02:36.950 Instead of using a single reasoning style, it can assemble a chain of small reasoning steps tailored 02:36.950 --> 02:38.630 to the specific problem.
  • 02:38.750 --> 02:45.310 This makes the model more flexible as the agent figures out the optimal course of action automatically.

Lesson 98: Human-in-the-loop

00:05.480 --> 00:08.320 Do you remember studying math in high school? 00:08.760 --> 00:15.480 Sometimes you'd start a problem with the wrong assumption, and every step after that would be affected 00:15.480 --> 00:16.280 by the end.

Core Concept

Do you remember studying math in high school? Sometimes you'd start a problem with the wrong assumption, and every step after that would be affected by the end. The teacher no longer deducted points for a single mistake.

Key Points

  • Instead, they often marked the entire solution as wrong.
  • AI agents often face a similar challenge.
  • They tend to commit to a solution prematurely without adequately exploring the best approach.
  • Once an LLM begins reasoning down the wrong path, the error can snowball, producing a final result that diverges significantly from the intended outcome.
  • In such instances, it's beneficial if the AI agent can receive guidance.
  • Such help can come in two forms one through self-reflection as discussed in the previous lesson, or two through feedback from a human.
  • People possess specialized skills and intuition that make them far better at correcting an agent's course and helping the AI reach its goal.
  • Moreover, human directions help the AI produce a result that aligns with human expectations.
💡 From the Lecture
00:05.480 --> 00:08.320 Do you remember studying math in high school?
Key Takeaways
  • 01:56.410 --> 02:02.730 Human involvement provides a critical safeguard, ensuring that the agent's reasoning remains aligned 02:02.730 --> 02:03.810 with reality.
  • 02:04.250 --> 02:10.210 Moreover, we shouldn't forget that it's always best practice to add a human in the loop.
  • 02:10.690 --> 02:18.170 Human oversight can help agents recover when they reach a dead end or become trapped in repetitive reasoning.
  • 02:18.370 --> 02:25.650 By offering external feedback or correction, a human can redirect the agent's reasoning and help it 02:25.690 --> 02:28.690 continue toward a productive solution.

Lesson 100: Guardrails and Policy Enforcement

00:05.400 --> 00:08.360 Why do we need guardrails on roads? 00:09.200 --> 00:12.000 They prevent cars from veering off cliffs. 00:12.240 --> 00:12.720 Right. 00:13.080 --> 00:16.000 This approach reduces the risk for drivers.

Core Concept

Why do we need guardrails on roads? They prevent cars from veering off cliffs. Right.

Key Points

  • This approach reduces the risk for drivers.
  • But it's not the only mechanism that does so.
  • There are also speed limits that regulate how fast drivers can travel, reducing the likelihood of losing control.
  • Similarly, traffic lights guide the flow of vehicles, minimizing collisions at intersections.
  • Road signs provide critical information about hazards ahead, enabling drivers to anticipate and avoid danger.
  • So road safety is created by combining several layered mechanisms.
  • While a single mechanism is unlikely to provide sufficient protection, using multiple specialized mechanisms together improves the system as a whole and helps mitigate risks.
  • Similarly, when creating AI agents, we must ensure that necessary guardrails for protection are in place.
💡 From the Lecture
02:57.910 --> 03:05.270 Once an AI agent is deployed in real world situations, new edges will inevitably emerge, requiring 03:05.270 --> 03:09.510 you to update and refine its guardrails continually.
Key Takeaways

  • 02:51.150 --> 02:57.550 Building robust guardrails is an ongoing process, one that's never truly finished.

Lesson 101: Cost-limiter

00:05.880 --> 00:11.480 If there's one thing that makes businesses uneasy, it's cost uncertainty. 00:12.240 --> 00:19.160 The thought of deploying a solution that consumes resources 24 over seven, while having little idea 00:19.160 --> 00:24.880 what the month end bill will be until it arrives, must be unsettling for management.

Core Concept

If there's one thing that makes businesses uneasy, it's cost uncertainty. The thought of deploying a solution that consumes resources 24 over seven, while having little idea what the month end bill will be until it arrives, must be unsettling for management. This is vastly different from what they've seen so far.

Key Points

  • With traditional software cost limiter execution time can vary, but within acceptable limits.
  • The cost of development personnel remains relatively stable, while deployment and maintenance expenses are minimal compared to the initial investment.
  • As a result, company executives can gauge their costs with a high degree of certainty before getting started.
  • This isn't necessarily true for AI agents, which operate 24 over seven.
  • One of their key advantages and can make thousands of API and LM calls each day.
  • They can get stuck in a loop over query APIs and generate strange and expensive outputs.
  • To address this issue, AI engineers must design systems with safeguards that prevent agents from incurring excessive costs without explicit authorization.
  • This technique, known as cost limiter, acts as a governance mechanism that ensures the agent operates within a predefined budget.
💡 From the Lecture
01:25.450 --> 01:28.210 All of this means higher bills.
💡 From the Lecture
01:51.970 --> 01:59.490 In practice, the cost limiter can be set for the agent in terms of tokens, dollars, or the number 01:59.490 --> 02:00.850 of API calls.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:01.890 --> 02:05.250 And what happens when an agent reaches its spending limit?
  • 02:05.810 --> 02:13.570 It shuts down gracefully and delivers a helpful fallback response, letting the user know it cannot 02:13.570 --> 02:14.370 continue.
  • 02:15.130 --> 02:21.490 For example, suppose this occurs with a call service agent once the cost limiter is reached during 02:21.490 --> 02:22.450 a conversation.
  • 02:22.930 --> 02:28.650 In that case, the agent can escalate the interaction to a human operator to take over.

Lesson 102: A/B Shadow Testing

00:10.720 --> 00:16.800 Customers are using it, and you observe their interactions and gain valuable insights on what could 00:16.800 --> 00:17.760 be improved. 00:18.440 --> 00:23.800 After a while, it becomes evident that the AI agent needs a few tweaks.

Core Concept

Let's say your AI agent is already deployed in production. Customers are using it, and you observe their interactions and gain valuable insights on what could be improved. After a while, it becomes evident that the AI agent needs a few tweaks.

Key Points

  • This type of system, however, is far from an exact science.
  • New versions don't always guarantee better performance, and when clients interact with the product in real life situations, you don't want to risk degrading their experience by rolling out an unproven update.
  • This is where AB shadow testing comes into play.
  • As with a typical AB test, we'll compare two versions, the original A and the new version B, but to ensure the user experience remains unchanged, we won't display the new version to users.
  • Everyone will continue seeing the original version.
  • The new version will exist only in the background, running in a shadow environment.
  • The agent receives user inputs and produces outputs, but those outputs remain hidden from the end users.
  • Instead, they're logged and compared with the original versions.
💡 From the Lecture
00:05.600 --> 00:10.280 Let's say your AI agent is already deployed in production.
Key Takeaways
  • 01:32.230 --> 01:33.190 Responses.
  • 01:33.910 --> 01:41.350 This allows us to closely observe how the new version performs under real traffic conditions, with 01:41.350 --> 01:47.910 the same users prompts and context, without risking the actual customer experience.
  • 01:48.790 --> 01:55.430 After collecting the results from the new shadow version, we can analyze the data to understand how 01:55.430 --> 02:03.630 the changes impacted the agent's performance, including latency, accuracy, compliance with governance 02:03.630 --> 02:06.670 rules, and overall user experience.
  • 02:07.350 --> 02:14.830 Ideally, the results indicate that the new version is reliable, making it suitable for a gradual rollout 02:14.870 --> 02:16.350 to production users.

Lesson 103: Bias and Fairness Systems

Core Concept

One key difference between LMS and agents is that agents can act. Therefore, any bias and fairness concerns we have are magnified many times over when it comes to agents with LMS. The output is text that the users read and interpret.

  • While biased responses are a serious concern.
  • Humans can still evaluate the text and judge its usefulness.
  • Agents, on the other hand, are autonomous and can change the environment.
  • Their biases don't just stay confined to words on a screen.
  • An agent's capacity to take action is its greatest advantage, but it also amplifies potential risks, since even minor reasoning biases can rapidly lead to real world consequences.
  • Furthermore, once an LLM is placed within an agentic framework, the potential for errors increases as it becomes connected to external data sources.
  • tools, and possibly other agents, creating many additional points where issues can arise.
  • It's not just the LM you need to worry about, but the entire system.

Lesson 105: How to Measure Agent Performance

00:05.720 --> 00:14.760 When evaluating agent performance, several critical dimensions come to mind accuracy, cost, latency, 00:15.240 --> 00:20.160 safety, and ultimately overall user experience. 00:20.720 --> 00:28.200 This means we can't focus on a single metric in isolation, just as we wouldn't judge a car solely by 00:28.200 --> 00:36.000 its speed, but instead consider factors like fuel efficiency, safety, reliability, and comfort.

Core Concept

When evaluating agent performance, several critical dimensions come to mind accuracy, cost, latency, safety, and ultimately overall user experience. This means we can't focus on a single metric in isolation, just as we wouldn't judge a car solely by its speed, but instead consider factors like fuel efficiency, safety, reliability, and comfort. Evaluating AI agents requires balancing multiple dimensions rather than optimizing for just one.

Key Points

  • Increasing in agent's accuracy, for instance, might come at the cost of higher latency.
  • User satisfaction is crucial, but it must be balanced against operational expenses.
  • Likewise, a perfect, reliable system is of little value if it isn't safe for end users.
  • Each of these factors is interconnected, and it's essential to understand how they influence one another within the context of the specific use case.
  • The North Star metric, or in other words, the primary KPI to track, will differ from one use case to another.
  • If you're developing a trading agent, chances are accuracy will be your top priority.
  • The team developing an agent that interacts with high value clients will likely focus intensely on customer satisfaction and user experience.
  • We must also account for how these dimensions interact.
💡 From the Lecture
00:20.720 --> 00:28.200 This means we can't focus on a single metric in isolation, just as we wouldn't judge a car solely by 00:28.200 --> 00:36.000 its speed, but instead consider factors like fuel efficiency, safety, reliability, and comfort.
💡 From the Lecture
00:47.280 --> 00:53.280 Increasing in agent's accuracy, for instance, might come at the cost of higher latency.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:06.270 --> 02:13.910 Recognizing that beyond a certain level of optimization, improvements in one area almost always come 02:13.910 --> 02:15.550 at the expense of another.
  • 02:15.870 --> 02:20.790 The key is to strike the right balance for the specific use case.
  • 02:21.110 --> 02:27.310 In the following two lessons, we'll outline practical steps for measuring agent performance.
  • 02:27.590 --> 02:28.870 Thanks for watching.

Lesson 106: Offline Benchmarks

00:05.680 --> 00:13.160 A few lessons ago, we introduced the concept of ab shadow testing, a method used when companies want 00:13.160 --> 00:20.440 to avoid risking the user experience by exposing users to the output of a new, untested agent.

Core Concept

A few lessons ago, we introduced the concept of ab shadow testing, a method used when companies want to avoid risking the user experience by exposing users to the output of a new, untested agent. The concept of offline evaluation is similar. It involves measuring an agent's performance under controlled test conditions using curated datasets and predefined scenarios.

Key Points

  • Imagine you've developed a customer support agent for an e-commerce company.
  • Instead of immediately allowing it to interact with real customers, you first test it on a dataset of 500 past support tickets.
  • Each ticket is already labeled with the correct response or action, allowing you to compare the agent's output against this predefined gold standard.
  • This approach allows you to estimate the agent's success rate, including accuracy and error rate, before it ever interacts with real customers.
  • Today, several tools can automate this evaluation process.
  • Among them are lang, chain, evals, and helm.
  • The clear advantage is that it eliminates any risk of negatively impacting the experience of your existing users.
  • The drawback is that the data used is historical and may not accurately represent current business conditions.
💡 From the Lecture
00:36.520 --> 00:41.160 Imagine you've developed a customer support agent for an e-commerce company.
💡 From the Lecture
02:01.610 --> 02:08.290 They act as a guiding framework for the team, highlighting which areas require optimization before 02:08.290 --> 02:12.570 the agent is ready for deployment in real world situations.

  • 01:42.410 --> 01:50.290 As a result, the effectiveness of offline benchmarks depends heavily on the quality and relevance of 01:50.290 --> 01:52.090 the sample data you select.

Lesson 107: Online Metrics

00:05.640 --> 00:13.360 If the product is already live, we can consider deploying our new AI agent directly into production 00:13.360 --> 00:15.480 for interaction with real users. 00:16.240 --> 00:23.200 We've discussed the drawbacks of this approach in detail, but there are situations where it's simply 00:23.200 --> 00:24.080 unavoidable.

Core Concept

If the product is already live, we can consider deploying our new AI agent directly into production for interaction with real users. We've discussed the drawbacks of this approach in detail, but there are situations where it's simply unavoidable. There are cases where no amount of offline testing can fully replicate the unpredictability of real world user interactions.

Key Points

  • We can't simply launch the agent and hope everything will be fine.
  • Instead, we should focus on several online metrics that reveal how the agent performs across its thousands of interactions.
  • Typically, you'd want to track the following metrics.
  • User satisfaction indicators and business KPIs such as sales, renewals, subscriptions, and similar outcomes.
  • Here's an example of how a business might use these indicators.
  • Aerocom has just launched a new real estate app featuring an agent that can search all the latest listings in town and find properties that match a user's criteria.
  • Since Aero is a startup and this functionality is brand new with no historical data or prior interactions to test against, the company plans to deploy the agent live and monitor key metrics to ensure it performs as intended.
  • The metrics Aerocom has chosen to track include task success rate, how often users successfully find suitable properties using the app.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:40.450 --> 02:47.490 Only by examining all the indicators together can we gain a complete understanding of how the agent 02:47.490 --> 02:48.410 is performing.
  • 02:49.130 --> 02:54.490 Similarly, we should monitor multiple KPIs that reflect the agent's performance.
  • 02:55.010 --> 03:00.450 Since this occurs in a live production environment where real users are affected.
  • 03:00.810 --> 03:08.930 It's crucial to respond quickly and implement fixes as soon as any correctable issue arises.

Lesson 112: Tokens

00:14.000 --> 00:15.080 There's no time to waste. 00:19.280 --> 00:25.520 You've likely used ChatGPT and know it works by sending a prompt to the model and expecting a text answer. 00:26.120 --> 00:29.840 The question is how does the model make sense of this text?

Core Concept

Welcome back, everyone to this section on tokens, OpenAI models and model pricing. There's no time to waste. So let's kick things off by discussing tokens.

Key Points

  • You've likely used ChatGPT and know it works by sending a prompt to the model and expecting a text answer.
  • The question is how does the model make sense of this text?
  • How does it understand the meaning of the words and their mutual connection?
  • This, of course, is a challenging question to answer, but in this lesson we'll look at one aspect that makes this possible tokenization.
  • Tokenization is a process whereby text inputs and outputs are broken down into sequences of characters called tokens.
  • The unique tokens that an LLM operates form the vocabulary of this LM, a token amounts to roughly three quarters of a word.
  • An easier way of remembering this is to consider that 100 tokens corresponds to approximately 75 words.
  • So when talking about OpenAI's tokenizing mechanism, a token isn't necessarily a single character or a word, but rather a sequence of characters frequently seen together.
💡 From the Lecture
02:22.850 --> 02:28.370 As you can imagine, predicting the next word in a sentence is easier than predicting the next character.
💡 From the Lecture
02:37.450 --> 02:41.890 Imagine we defined a token roughly as a sentence rather than a word.
Key Takeaways

Lesson 116: Setting the API Key as an Environment Variable

00:08.040 --> 00:15.280 Hey, in the previous lesson, we logged into OpenAI's website, generated a personal API key, and 00:15.280 --> 00:17.240 saved it locally in a text file. 00:18.120 --> 00:23.200 We'll learn how to set this API key as an environment variable, which will soon be used to communicate 00:23.200 --> 00:24.920 with the OpenAI library.

Core Concept

Hey, in the previous lesson, we logged into OpenAI's website, generated a personal API key, and saved it locally in a text file. We'll learn how to set this API key as an environment variable, which will soon be used to communicate with the OpenAI library. First, let's delve into the concept of environment variables.

Key Points

  • An environment variable is a key value pair used by the operating system, with the key corresponding to the name of the variable, while the value representing, in our case the OpenAI API key.
  • The key and the value are typically stored as strings.
  • A classic example is the path environment variable, which stores a list of directories where executable programs are located, enabling the operating system to find these programs when needed.
  • Another typical example is the home or home path environment variable, storing the path to the user's home directory.
  • Environment variables are essential for protecting such sensitive data as API keys.
  • For example, the OpenAI API key, a required credential for accessing the OpenAI services, should not be exposed within the code.
  • Hard coding its value risks unintended exposure, such as when you share your code with friends or colleagues.
  • This is a critical security issue because invoking OpenAI's models through the API corresponds to using tokens, a paid service.
💡 From the Lecture

💻 Code Walkthrough: 04-The-OpenAI-API-01.ipynb

First Steps

Welcome back to the course everyone! In the previous section, we used the Anaconda Prompt to create a new environment called langchain_env. As emphasized, it’s recommended that individual projects be run in separate environments to prevent package conflicts or the accidental removal of important documents. They also offer the flexibility to install different Python versions and maintain unique package sets in each without the risk of interfering with the base setup. We also registered this environment as a Jupyter kernel so that we could use it in our Jupyter notebooks. Finally, we set our OpenAI API key as an environment variable, allowing us to utilize OpenAI’s models and API. I’m now happy to welcome you to this lesson, where we’ll create our first chatbot. We’ll be relying on Python and OpenAI’s API. Note that we won’t be making use of the LangChain framework just yet. This section introduces you to creating chatbots with OpenAI’s API and familiarizes you with its main components. Since OpenAI’s integration in LangChain relies heavily on this API, having a general idea of how it works is valuable. With that said, let’s get to coding! 😊 Load the dotenv extension and then apply the %dotenv magic command to set your OpenAI API key as an environment variable.

Next, we should configure the OpenAI library to recognize our key. To do so, import the os and openai libraries.

Step 1 
import os
import openai

Then, set openai.api_key to equal os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY'), passing the name of the environment variable as an argument.

Step 2 
openai.api_key = os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY')

We’re now ready to experiment with OpenAI’s models. We’ll do so by implementing a helpful chatbot that answers users’ questions. But we’ll also give it a sarcastic twist. 😊 First, create an OpenAI client by utilizing OpenAI’s class of the same name.

Step 3 
client = openai.OpenAI()

Then, define a completion variable that will serve as our chatbot object. Set it equal to client.chat.completions.create. The first parameter that the create() function requires is the model. I’ll opt for GPT-4, but you can experiment with any OpenAI chat model. Just visit their website, pick a language model of your choice, and write the respective name as a string. Keep in mind our discussion about costs—especially if you plan on working on your own projects. Make sure you opt for a cost-sensitive variant. The second required parameter (messages) contains the messages we’ll give the model before starting the conversation. These messages will be a way to instruct the model on how to behave. It expects a list of dictionaries, each containing two required key-value pairs.

Step 4 
completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{}, 
                                                        {}])

The key to the first pair is ‘role,’ which can be mapped to one of the following values: ‘system,’ ‘user,’ ‘assistant,’ and ‘tool.’ We’ll work with tools later in the course. For now, let’s focus on the first three. The key to the second pair is ‘content,’ which stores strings with questions, instructions, or other helpful content that will guide the model towards responding suitably. All right! Next, we’ll discuss the difference between system, user, and assistant roles. Catch you in a bit! 😊

Key Takeaways
  • 03:32.280 --> 03:37.640 The key to the second pair is content, which stores strings with questions, instructions, and other 03:37.640 --> 03:41.120 helpful content that will guide the model towards responding suitably.
  • 03:42.520 --> 03:43.160 All right.
  • 03:43.480 --> 03:48.200 After a short break, we'll discuss the difference between system, user and assistant roles.
  • 03:49.240 --> 03:50.120 Catch you in a bit.

Lesson 118: System, User, and Assistant Roles

00:07.360 --> 00:08.160 Hey everyone! 00:09.000 --> 00:15.200 Last time we started creating our chat completion object, we left it off at the messages parameter, 00:15.480 --> 00:20.680 a list of dictionaries where we can specify prompts as a system, a user or an assistant.

Core Concept

Hey everyone! Last time we started creating our chat completion object, we left it off at the messages parameter, a list of dictionaries where we can specify prompts as a system, a user or an assistant. Let's now discuss each of these roles individually.

Key Points

  • The system role is typically used for directing the model.
  • It defines the model's purpose, persona, output, format, and any other necessary instructions.
  • Providing the bot with a system message guarantees a better response for your specific use case.
  • For instance, if you were to create a grammar corrector, an appropriate system message would be you will be provided with statements and your task is to convert them to standard English.
  • If you were to create a chatbot with a sarcastic twist instead, you could give it the following instructions.
  • You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly answers questions with sarcastic responses.
  • For more ideas on possible system prompts, refer to OpenAI's web page.
  • The second role on our list is the user role.

💻 Code Walkthrough: 04-The-OpenAI-API-03.ipynb

Creating a Sarcastic Chatbot

Welcome back, everyone! In this lesson, we’ll resume the implementation of our chat completion in Jupyter Notebook. We’ll start by instructing the chatbot to answer questions sarcastically through a system message and then pass our question as a user-role message. Let’s get into it! For starters, run the first four code cells below.

Step 1 
import os
import openai
Step 2 
openai.api_key = os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY')
Step 3 
client = openai.OpenAI()

Now, the first dictionary in our messages list should map the ‘role’ keyword to ‘system’, implying a system message. In addition, set the content to the one already familiar to you: *You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly answers questions with sarcastic responses.* In the second dictionary in the list, we’ll create a user message. I’ll go with the following request: *I’ve recently adopted a dog. Could you suggest some dog names?*

Step 4 
completion = client.chat.completions.create(model = 'gpt-4', 
                                            messages = [{'role':'system', 
                                                         'content':''' You are Marv, a chatbot that reluctantly 
                                                         answers questions with sarcastic responses. '''}, 
                                                        {'role':'user', 
                                                         'content':''' I've recently adopted a dog. 
                                                         Could you suggest some dog names? '''}])

Run the cell above and inspect the completion variable.

Step 5 
completion

We find that completion is an instance of the ChatCompletion class, with the parameter choices storing a list of Choice objects that, in turn, keep the responses from the chatbot. By default, the model returns only one response, which is typically the desired setting. This number can be controlled through a parameter called n. Of course, more responses result in higher token consumption and, therefore, higher cost. The role assigned to this message is ‘assistant.’ Additionally, information is available on the number of completion, prompt, and total tokens.

Finally, for this lesson, let’s check how the chatbot responded by displaying the output in a more readable form. To do that:

  • first, retrieve the choices list from the ChatCompletion object,
  • then select the first and only item in this list,
  • fetch the messages parameter from the Choice object,
  • and lastly, extract the content from the ChatCompletionMessage object.
Make sure you apply the print-function to the string to ensure the message is nicely formatted.

Step 6 
print(completion.choices[0].message.content)

Excellent job, everyone. In the upcoming lesson, we’ll discuss additional parameters that can help further control the model’s response. See you in a bit!

Lesson 120: Temperature, Max Tokens, and Streaming

00:10.760 --> 00:15.480 We then used a system message to create a chatbot that adopts a sarcastic persona. 00:30.880 --> 00:36.360 As discussed earlier, OpenAI sets its model prices based on the number of input tokens.

Core Concept

Welcome back. In this section, we've discussed the roles we can employ when passing a message to a model, a system user or assistant role. We then used a system message to create a chatbot that adopts a sarcastic persona.

Key Points

  • As discussed earlier, OpenAI sets its model prices based on the number of input tokens.
  • The ones we feed to the model and the number of completion tokens those the model generates.
  • Both are capped to prevent users from inputting an excessive number of tokens, and to stop the models from generating endless text.
  • Still, it's essential to have additional control over the amount of text generated.
  • Models often tend to be wordy and provide more information than needed.
  • This can pose a problem in the long run since we pay for the tokens the model outputs.
  • As a side note, this pricing only applies when using OpenAI's models through the API.
  • In contrast, the ChatGPT platform is subscription based rather than token based, and you don't need to worry about the model generating long texts.
