Core Concept

We start by creating a single user message inside the content. We add our request. I'll ask the agent to read the CV that sits in the same folder as this notebook, and compare it with three job postings.

Key Points

  • We pass this into the compiled graph, and I'll store the output in a separate variable so we don't overwrite the input.
  • And then we can print each message to see exactly what happened.
  • And we can now see through the entire process step by step.
  • Currently running another request with the react graph won't retain our previous messages.
  • Each run starts fresh to make our agent remember past interactions and keep the conversation flowing naturally.
  • We'll need to use a memory enabled graph with a stable thread ID.
  • That's precisely what we'll do in our next lecture.

@tool
def job_posting_tool(job_link: str) -> str:
    """Extracts structured information from a job posting at the provided URL.

    Args:
        job_link (str): The URL of the job posting.

    Returns:
        str: A structured summary of the job posting's key details.
    """
    completion = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-search-preview",
        web_search_options={"search_context_size": "medium"},
        messages=[
            {
            "role": "user",
            "content": """
            You are a helpful tool that visits the following job posting and carefully read its contents.  
            Summarize the key details in a clear and concise format, including:
            Visit the provided job posting link, read it thoroughly, and extract and summarize all key information. Include:
            - Job title
            - Company name
            - Location
            - Employment type (full-time, part-time, contract, etc.)
            - Salary or compensation (if available)
            - Required qualifications/skills
            - Primary responsibilities
            - Benefits offered
            - Application instructions
            - Posting date (if available)

            Format
            - Respond with a clear, structured bullet-point list.
            - Use exact factual information from the posting, no rewording beyond making it concise.
            - If the posting is missing, inaccessible, or contains no job details, respond with:
            "Job posting unavailable or contains no job details."

            Do's 
            - Ensure all extracted details are accurate and directly taken from the posting.
            - Keep descriptions short, professional, and easy to scan.
            - Use consistent formatting for all fields (e.g., “Job Title: …”).  
            Don'ts
            - Do not include filler language, speculation, or personal opinions.
            - Do not rewrite or interpret details—only report factual information from the posting.
            """
        },
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": f"Visit this job posting and extract details:\n{job_link}"
        }
    ],
    )
    return completion.choices[0].message.content
Step 5 
@tool
def extract_cv_text(file_path: str) -> str:
    """Extracts the text content from a CV file in PDF, DOCX, or DOC format. The CV should be inside the same folder that this notebook is in.

    Args:
        file_path (str): The local file path to the CV document. 

    Returns:
        str: The extracted plain text from the CV, or an error message if the format is unsupported or cannot be read.
    """
    
    ext = os.path.splitext(file_path)[-1].lower()
    
    if ".docx" in ext:
        try:
            doc = docx.Document(file_path)
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .docx file: {e}"
        
    elif ".pdf" in ext:
        try:
            text = []
            with pdfplumber.open(file_path) as pdf:
                for page in pdf.pages:
                    page_text = page.extract_text()
                    if page_text:
                        text.append(page_text)
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .pdf file: {e}"
    
    elif ".doc" in ext:
        try:
            temp_docx = file_path + ".temp.docx"
            subprocess.run(['soffice', '--headless', '--convert-to', 'docx', '--outdir', os.path.dirname(file_path), file_path], check=True)
            
            doc = docx.Document(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            
            os.remove(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading .doc file: {e}"
    
    else:
        return "Unsupported file format. Please use .pdf, .docx, or .doc."

Lesson 200: Adding Memory

00:00.760 --> 00:03.720 Right now, our agent has a bit of a goldfish memory. 00:04.080 --> 00:07.760 Every time we run it, it starts fresh and forgets anything we've said before. 00:08.240 --> 00:13.200 That's fine for one off questions, but for a real conversation, we need our assistant to remember 00:13.200 --> 00:15.400 context across multiple exchanges.

Core Concept

Right now, our agent has a bit of a goldfish memory. Every time we run it, it starts fresh and forgets anything we've said before. That's fine for one off questions, but for a real conversation, we need our assistant to remember context across multiple exchanges.

Key Points

  • Landgraf makes this possible with something called a check pointer, a storage system that keeps track of the graph state between runs.
  • Think of it like the agent's short term memory.
  • We'll start with the simplest built in check pointer memory saver.
  • Then we create it just like any other object.
  • The next step is to recompile our graph, but this time we pass in our check pointer.
  • By doing this, we're telling Landgraf, store the state for this graph and reuse it in the next time I call it.
  • We also need to tell Landgraf which conversation to keep track of.
  • This is where the stable thread ID comes in.
💡 From the Lecture
00:08.240 --> 00:13.200 That's fine for one off questions, but for a real conversation, we need our assistant to remember 00:13.200 --> 00:15.400 context across multiple exchanges.
💡 From the Lecture
00:24.560 --> 00:27.120 Think of it like the agent's short term memory.

Lesson 202: ReWOO Architecture Overview

00:07.640 --> 00:14.400 Up to this point, we've been building our agent using the react architecture and it's performed impressively. 00:15.080 --> 00:21.040 The react agent can think through problems, make decisions, call tools, observe results, and continue 00:21.040 --> 00:22.440 reasoning step by step.

Core Concept

Welcome to the next section of our course. Up to this point, we've been building our agent using the react architecture and it's performed impressively. The react agent can think through problems, make decisions, call tools, observe results, and continue reasoning step by step.

Key Points

  • Now it's time to change direction and explore a different kind of architecture.
  • At its core, Riwu separates planning from execution.
  • With react, the agent pauses after each action.
  • It thinks, acts, observes the outcome, and then repeats the cycle.
  • This approach is flexible, but it also forces the agent to constantly pause, wait for tool results, and reconsider its plan at every step.
  • Rather than reasoning step by step, it operates through three distinct phases one.
  • The planner node examines the user's request and creates a structured plan.
  • Instead of calling tools immediately, it anticipates which tools will be required, in what sequence and with which inputs.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:12.750 --> 02:15.830 This makes the process more efficient and easier to monitor.
  • 02:16.990 --> 02:22.510 The trade off is that this type of agent is less adaptive compared to a react agent, since it won't 02:22.510 --> 02:25.190 rethink halfway through if something changes.
  • 02:26.470 --> 02:28.870 Will this approach perform better than react?
  • 02:29.590 --> 02:32.550 Let's make the necessary changes to our project and find out.

Lesson 203: Building the Planner Node

00:10.200 --> 00:15.280 This approach allows it to serve as a reusable component within our lane graph workflow. 00:16.040 --> 00:18.440 First, we'll create a regex pattern. 00:21.560 --> 00:25.880 This regular expression is designed to parse the raw output of the planner prompt.

Core Concept

Now that we've tested the planner prompt and observed how it generates a structured plan, let's integrate that logic within a proper planner node function. This approach allows it to serve as a reusable component within our lane graph workflow. First, we'll create a regex pattern.

Key Points

  • This regular expression is designed to parse the raw output of the planner prompt.
  • With this part, we capture the text after the word plan.
  • The next part extracts the placeholder variable such as e1, for example.
  • Finally, we retrieve the tools input such as a file path or a URL in this case.
  • First we assign a name and pass in the state object, which we've called Riwu.
  • Next, we'll send the task along with the planner prompt to the LLM to generate the raw plan text.
  • Then we'll create a variable called steps, which uses the previously defined regex to extract and structure the response.
  • Finally, the function returns a dictionary with two elements one plan string which contains the raw text from the LLM, and two steps the structured version of the plan that the executor can follow.
💡 From the Lecture
00:30.920 --> 00:35.560 The next part extracts the placeholder variable such as e1, for example.

@traceable(name="Planner Node")
def planner_node(state: ReWOO):
    task = state["task"]
    raw_plan = llm.invoke(planner_prompt.format(task=task)).content
    steps = re.findall(plan_regex, raw_plan, flags=re.S)
    return {"plan_string": raw_plan, "steps": steps}

@tool
def job_posting_tool(job_link: str) -> str:
    """Extracts structured information from a job posting at the provided URL.

    Args:
        job_link (str): The URL of the job posting.

    Returns:
        str: A structured summary of the job posting's key details.
    """
    completion = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-search-preview",
        web_search_options={"search_context_size": "medium"},
        messages=[
            {
            "role": "user",
            "content": """
            You are a helpful tool that visits the following job posting and carefully read its contents.  
            Summarize the key details in a clear and concise format, including:
            Visit the provided job posting link, read it thoroughly, and extract and summarize all key information. Include:
            - Job title
            - Company name
            - Location
            - Employment type (full-time, part-time, contract, etc.)
            - Salary or compensation (if available)
            - Required qualifications/skills
            - Primary responsibilities
            - Benefits offered
            - Application instructions
            - Posting date (if available)

            Format
            - Respond with a clear, structured bullet-point list.
            - Use exact factual information from the posting, no rewording beyond making it concise.
            - If the posting is missing, inaccessible, or contains no job details, respond with:
            "Job posting unavailable or contains no job details."

            Do's 
            - Ensure all extracted details are accurate and directly taken from the posting.
            - Keep descriptions short, professional, and easy to scan.
            - Use consistent formatting for all fields (e.g., “Job Title: …”).  
            Don'ts
            - Do not include filler language, speculation, or personal opinions.
            - Do not rewrite or interpret details—only report factual information from the posting.
            """
        },
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": f"Visit this job posting and extract details:\n{job_link}"
        }
    ],
    )
    return completion.choices[0].message.content

@tool
def extract_cv_text(file_path: str) -> str:
    """Extracts the text content from a CV file in PDF, DOCX, or DOC format. The CV should be inside the same folder that this notebook is in.

    Args:
        file_path (str): The local file path to the CV document. 

    Returns:
        str: The extracted plain text from the CV, or an error message if the format is unsupported or cannot be read.
    """
    
    ext = os.path.splitext(file_path)[-1].lower()
    
    if ".docx" in ext:
        try:
            doc = docx.Document(file_path)
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .docx file: {e}"
        
    elif ".pdf" in ext:
        try:
            text = []
            with pdfplumber.open(file_path) as pdf:
                for page in pdf.pages:
                    page_text = page.extract_text()
                    if page_text:
                        text.append(page_text)
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .pdf file: {e}"
    
    elif ".doc" in ext:
        try:
            temp_docx = file_path + ".temp.docx"
            subprocess.run(['soffice', '--headless', '--convert-to', 'docx', '--outdir', os.path.dirname(file_path), file_path], check=True)
            
            doc = docx.Document(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            
            os.remove(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading .doc file: {e}"
    
    else:
        return "Unsupported file format. Please use .pdf, .docx, or .doc."

Lesson 204: Implementing the Executor

00:01.400 --> 00:02.400 We're doing great. 00:02.640 --> 00:04.520 We're making excellent progress. 00:05.080 --> 00:10.240 Next, we'll clean up the code by removing components that are no longer required from the react build.

Core Concept

Okay. We're doing great. We're making excellent progress.

Key Points

  • Next, we'll clean up the code by removing components that are no longer required from the react build.
  • In react, the LM operated in a loop controlled by a tool node and a tool's condition in Rwu.
  • However, the executor calls tools directly based on the planner steps, so there's no need for an automatic tool calling loop.
  • We'll also remove the assistant node and its system prompt, since the assistant role is now handled by three dedicated nodes planner, executor, and solver.
  • First, we'll create a small helper function that determines which step we're currently on.
  • It does this by counting the number of pieces of evidence that have already been collected, and comparing that number to the total number of steps in the plan.
  • If all steps are complete, the helper returns none.
  • Otherwise, it returns the index of the next step to run.

02:35.580 --> 02:40.060 For example, the planner might tell the LM to use E1 as part of its reasoning.

def _current_index(state: ReWOO):
    done = len(state.get("results", {}))
    total = len(state["steps"])
    return None if done >= total else done
Step 17 
@traceable(name="Executor Node")
def executor_node(state: ReWOO):
    idx = _current_index(state)
    if idx is None:
        return {}
    plan_text, step_name, tool_name, tool_input = state["steps"][idx]
    for k, v in state.get("results", {}).items():
           if tool_name == "LLM" and k in tool_input:
               tool_input = tool_input.replace(k, v)

    if tool_name == "LLM":
        out = llm.invoke(tool_input).content
    elif tool_name == "CV":
        out = extract_cv_text.invoke(tool_input)
    elif tool_name == "JobPost":
        out = job_posting_tool.invoke(tool_input)
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown tool {tool_name}")

    results = dict(state.get("results", {}))
    results[step_name] = str(out)
    return {"results": results}

Lesson 205: Implementing the Solver

00:00.680 --> 00:06.360 Now that we have both the planner and the executor, it's time for the final piece of the puzzle the 00:06.360 --> 00:06.920 solver. 00:07.680 --> 00:14.200 Its role is simple yet critical to gather all the collected evidence and synthesize it into a clear, 00:14.200 --> 00:15.400 polished answer.

Core Concept

Now that we have both the planner and the executor, it's time for the final piece of the puzzle the solver. Its role is simple yet critical to gather all the collected evidence and synthesize it into a clear, polished answer. Let's start by creating the solver prompt.

Key Points

  • First, we remind the LM of its objective to use the plan and the collected evidence to solve the task.
  • Next, we include a placeholder called Plan block, where all the steps and their corresponding evidence will be inserted.
  • Finally, we restate the original task at the end to keep the model focused and maintain clarity.
  • After that, we'll construct the actual solver node.
  • Inside, we start by creating a list named lines.
  • It'll hold neatly formatted pieces of information, each pairing a planned step with its corresponding evidence.
  • We loop through each step in the plan for each step, we retrieve the plan description along with the evidence gathered by the executor.
  • Then we format them into a clear, readable string and add it to lines.

@tool
def job_posting_tool(job_link: str) -> str:
    """Extracts structured information from a job posting at the provided URL.

    Args:
        job_link (str): The URL of the job posting.

    Returns:
        str: A structured summary of the job posting's key details.
    """
    completion = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-search-preview",
        web_search_options={"search_context_size": "medium"},
        messages=[
            {
            "role": "user",
            "content": """
            You are a helpful tool that visits the following job posting and carefully read its contents.  
            Summarize the key details in a clear and concise format, including:
            Visit the provided job posting link, read it thoroughly, and extract and summarize all key information. Include:
            - Job title
            - Company name
            - Location
            - Employment type (full-time, part-time, contract, etc.)
            - Salary or compensation (if available)
            - Required qualifications/skills
            - Primary responsibilities
            - Benefits offered
            - Application instructions
            - Posting date (if available)

            Format
            - Respond with a clear, structured bullet-point list.
            - Use exact factual information from the posting, no rewording beyond making it concise.
            - If the posting is missing, inaccessible, or contains no job details, respond with:
            "Job posting unavailable or contains no job details."

            Do's 
            - Ensure all extracted details are accurate and directly taken from the posting.
            - Keep descriptions short, professional, and easy to scan.
            - Use consistent formatting for all fields (e.g., “Job Title: …”).  
            Don'ts
            - Do not include filler language, speculation, or personal opinions.
            - Do not rewrite or interpret details—only report factual information from the posting.
            """
        },
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": f"Visit this job posting and extract details:\n{job_link}"
        }
    ],
    )
    return completion.choices[0].message.content
Step 11 
@tool
def extract_cv_text(file_path: str) -> str:
    """Extracts the text content from a CV file in PDF, DOCX, or DOC format. The CV should be inside the same folder that this notebook is in.

    Args:
        file_path (str): The local file path to the CV document. 

    Returns:
        str: The extracted plain text from the CV, or an error message if the format is unsupported or cannot be read.
    """
    
    ext = os.path.splitext(file_path)[-1].lower()
    
    if ".docx" in ext:
        try:
            doc = docx.Document(file_path)
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .docx file: {e}"
        
    elif ".pdf" in ext:
        try:
            text = []
            with pdfplumber.open(file_path) as pdf:
                for page in pdf.pages:
                    page_text = page.extract_text()
                    if page_text:
                        text.append(page_text)
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading the .pdf file: {e}"
    
    elif ".doc" in ext:
        try:
            temp_docx = file_path + ".temp.docx"
            subprocess.run(['soffice', '--headless', '--convert-to', 'docx', '--outdir', os.path.dirname(file_path), file_path], check=True)
            
            doc = docx.Document(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            text = [para.text for para in doc.paragraphs]
            
            os.remove(os.path.splitext(file_path)[0] + ".docx")
            return '\n'.join(text)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error reading .doc file: {e}"
    
    else:
        return "Unsupported file format. Please use .pdf, .docx, or .doc."

Solve the following task or problem. To solve the problem, we have made step-by-step Plan and 
retrieved corresponding Evidence to each Plan. Use them with caution since long evidence might 
contain irrelevant information.

{plan_block}

Step 19 
@traceable(name="Solver Node")
def solver_node(state: ReWOO):
    lines = []
    for plan_text, step_name, tool_name, tool_input in state["steps"]:
        evidence = state["results"][step_name]
        lines.append(f"Plan: {plan_text}\nEvidence {step_name}: {evidence}\n")
    prompt = solver_promp.format(plan_block="\n".join(lines), task=state["task"])
    answer = llm.invoke(prompt).content.strip()
    return {"result": answer}

Lesson 206: Wiring Up the ReWOO Graph

00:03.360 --> 00:08.440 We'll go through it line by line, explaining each change from the react setup and the reasoning behind 00:08.440 --> 00:08.760 it. 00:09.280 --> 00:14.160 We'll begin with a router function, which determines the next step of the graph after each executor 00:14.160 --> 00:15.280 completes its run.

Core Concept

We'll go through it line by line, explaining each change from the react setup and the reasoning behind it. We'll begin with a router function, which determines the next step of the graph after each executor completes its run. If no steps remain, the process moves to the solver.

Key Points

  • We import the libraries previously used for the start and end state graph.
  • Note that the state graph we're about to initialize contains the Riwu state, not the Chatmessage state used in react.
  • We created the plan, the tool, and the solver and assign each its corresponding name.
  • Rather than using the start constant to add an edge as we did in the react project, we'll demonstrate an alternative method to show that there are multiple ways to define the starting point of a graph.
  • This time we'll use the set Entrypoint method to do it.
  • We're specifying where the graph should begin, but here we're explicitly designating the planner as the first action.
  • This fits nicely with Rewa's idea of starting with a clear plan before moving into execution.
  • From the plan, the process always proceeds to the executor for the first step.
💡 From the Lecture
01:54.460 --> 01:59.500 Now we must test it and verify that it functions correctly across various use cases.
💡 From the Lecture
02:46.940 --> 02:52.140 In the next lesson, we'll evaluate the results and determine which method works best for this use case.

Step 16 
def _current_index(state: ReWOO):
    done = len(state.get("results", {}))
    total = len(state["steps"])
    return None if done >= total else done
Step 17 
@traceable(name="Executor Node")
def executor_node(state: ReWOO):
    idx = _current_index(state)
    if idx is None:
        return {}
    plan_text, step_name, tool_name, tool_input = state["steps"][idx]
    for k, v in state.get("results", {}).items():
           if tool_name == "LLM" and k in tool_input:
               tool_input = tool_input.replace(k, v)

    if tool_name == "LLM":
        out = llm.invoke(tool_input).content
    elif tool_name == "CV":
        out = extract_cv_text.invoke(tool_input)
    elif tool_name == "JobPost":
        out = job_posting_tool.invoke(tool_input)
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown tool {tool_name}")

    results = dict(state.get("results", {}))
    results[step_name] = str(out)
    return {"results": results}
Step 18 
solver_promp = """
Solve the following task or problem. To solve the problem, we have made step-by-step Plan and 
retrieved corresponding Evidence to each Plan. Use them with caution since long evidence might 
contain irrelevant information.

{plan_block}

Now solve the question or task according to provided Evidence above. Respond with the answer
directly with no extra words.

Task: {task}
Response:

"""
Step 19 
@traceable(name="Solver Node")
def solver_node(state: ReWOO):
    lines = []
    for plan_text, step_name, tool_name, tool_input in state["steps"]:
        evidence = state["results"][step_name]
        lines.append(f"Plan: {plan_text}\nEvidence {step_name}: {evidence}\n")
    prompt = solver_promp.format(plan_block="\n".join(lines), task=state["task"])
    answer = llm.invoke(prompt).content.strip()
    return {"result": answer}
Step 20 
def router(state: ReWOO):
    return "solve" if _current_index(state) is None else "tool"
Step 21 
from langgraph.graph import START, StateGraph, END

builder = StateGraph(ReWOO)
builder.add_node("plan", planner_node)
builder.add_node("tool", executor_node)
builder.add_node("solve", solver_node)

builder.set_entry_point("plan")
builder.add_edge("plan", "tool")
builder.add_conditional_edges("tool", router)
builder.add_edge("solve", END)

Lesson 209: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)

00:09.880 --> 00:15.600 Human in the loop can take many forms depending on when and how people interact with the system, whether 00:15.600 --> 00:18.800 before, during, or after the AI makes a decision.

Core Concept

In this lesson, we'll take a deeper look at the concept of human in the loop. Human in the loop can take many forms depending on when and how people interact with the system, whether before, during, or after the AI makes a decision. Understanding these variations allows us to identify the type of human oversight most appropriate for each situation.

Key Points

  • In other words, understanding the human role in the loop enables us to strike the right balance between automation and human judgment.
  • Below are the main patterns found in agentic systems, along with guidance on when to use each one.
  • We'll begin with the most common configuration the human as verifier.
  • The AI agent completes a task, after which a human steps in to review, validate, and, if needed, correct the output.
  • After the agent received a thumbs up from the human, the process continues.
  • This approach is valuable when the agent is prone to subtle errors or when the stakes are high.
  • If you're developing a solution in the medical or legal field, achieving extremely high precision and output quality is essential.
  • In summary, using a human as the verifier is easy to implement, highly effective at catching subtle mistakes, and best suited for situations where stakes are high or strict compliance requirements.
💡 From the Lecture
00:27.200 --> 00:32.920 In other words, understanding the human role in the loop enables us to strike the right balance between 00:32.960 --> 00:34.880 automation and human judgment.
💡 From the Lecture
01:42.670 --> 01:48.350 Think of it like a pilot who can take manual control from the autopilot whenever something seems off.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:15.270 --> 02:21.270 In this setup, the agent can pause between reasoning steps to ask clarifying questions whenever uncertainty 02:21.310 --> 02:22.150 arises.
  • 02:23.270 --> 02:29.310 This mirrors how our project begins, with the system engaging the user through follow up questions.
  • 02:29.950 --> 02:36.030 Alright, in our next lesson, we'll explore parallelization and discover how it can make our system 02:36.030 --> 02:37.790 faster and more efficient.
  • 02:38.270 --> 02:39.030 Stay tuned.

Lesson 210: Parallelization

00:05.040 --> 00:10.960 In the previous lesson, we explored human in the loop concepts and the various strategies used to implement 00:10.960 --> 00:11.320 them. 00:14.880 --> 00:21.120 One of the key advantages of working with Landgraf the Landgraf framework makes it especially simple 00:21.120 --> 00:21.880 to implement.

Core Concept

In the previous lesson, we explored human in the loop concepts and the various strategies used to implement them. In this lesson, we'll discuss parallelization. One of the key advantages of working with Landgraf the Landgraf framework makes it especially simple to implement.

Key Points

  • But first, let me introduce you or remind you of the concept of parallelization.
  • At the core, parallelization enables multiple processes to run simultaneously rather than sequentially.
  • In traditional systems, tasks are executed one after another, each starting only after the previous one finishes.
  • But in many situations, especially when tasks are independent of each other, it's wasteful to wait.
  • Landgraf simplifies this by allowing nodes to run in parallel whenever they don't rely on each other's outputs.
  • The best part is how natural this feels in Landgraf.
  • Parallelization doesn't require complex thread management or specialized code.
  • All you need to do is connect multiple nodes to the same parent.
💡 From the Lecture
00:14.880 --> 00:21.120 One of the key advantages of working with Landgraf the Landgraf framework makes it especially simple 00:21.120 --> 00:21.880 to implement.
Key Takeaways
  • 02:17.420 --> 02:21.460 Since they're independent, we can send them all off at the same time.
  • 02:21.860 --> 02:27.020 Landgraf will then collect their outputs and feed them together into the next stage of the pipeline.
  • 02:27.620 --> 02:29.220 Our plan is set.
  • 02:29.620 --> 02:31.780 The next step is to start coding.

Core Concept

Let's start with the human in the loop part. As I described earlier, this is the short back and forth with the agent asks the founder for any missing details until it has enough context to proceed. We'll start by defining a system instruction for the loop.

Key Points

  • Next, we'll shift our focus to the decider.
  • This is the first node that runs after the start.
  • Prepends the system message, calls the model and returns the assistant's reply as a new message.
  • Since our messages field uses add underscore messages, returning a list with just the new AI message automatically appends it to the running conversation.
  • We need a router to determine where to go after the decider.
  • This function gives us full control over the branching logic.
  • First, we grab the last message by using the state messages minus one.
  • As you know, the minus one index in Python is how we get the last item in a sequence.

Lesson 214: Collection Node and Building the Graph

00:08.960 --> 00:12.720 We'll call this node collect and report at the top. 00:12.760 --> 00:14.440 Of course we add the state. 00:14.680 --> 00:17.120 Next we create a small safeguard. 00:17.600 --> 00:21.760 If fewer than four advisor reports are available, the node won't run.

Core Concept

Welcome back. Let's build the node that is responsible for collecting the outputs from the advisors and producing the final report. We'll call this node collect and report at the top.

Key Points

  • If fewer than four advisor reports are available, the node won't run.
  • This prevents the report from firing too early.
  • Once the reports are ready, we build a new prompt.
  • This tells the model to act as a senior consultant and combine all the advisor notes into one structured evaluation.
  • The advisor reports dictionary is injected directly into the prompt so the model has access to everything at once.
  • We display it nicely in markdown and return it under the final report key so it gets stored in the state.
  • We start by creating a state graph that knows about our state schema.
  • And this means we can register our nodes one by one, starting with the decider node.

from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

from IPython.display import Image, display, Markdown
Step 2 
llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o", temperature=0)
Step 3 
class State(TypedDict):
    idea: str
    messages: Annotated[List[BaseMessage], add_messages]
    advisor_reports: Annotated[Dict[str, str], operator.or_]
    final_report: str
Step 4 
base_system_msg = SystemMessage(
    content=(
        """
        You are a helpful tool
        Your job: decide whether you have enough information about the start-up idea.
        If not, ask ONE precise follow-up question.
        If yes, say: DONE
        """

    )
)
Step 5 
def decide_node(state: State):
    conversation = [base_system_msg] + state["messages"]
    ai_reply: AIMessage = llm(conversation)
    return {"messages": [ai_reply]}
Step 6 
def route(state: State):
    last_ai_msg: AIMessage = state["messages"][-1]
    if last_ai_msg.content.strip().upper().startswith("DONE"):
        return "fanout"
    return "ask_user_node"
Step 7 
def ask_user_node(state: State):
    question = state["messages"][-1].content
    print(f"\nAssistant: {question}\n")
    human = input("You: ")
    new_messages = state["messages"] + [HumanMessage(content=human)]
    
    return {"messages": new_messages,
            "human_advisor_feedback": human,}
Step 8 
def market_analyst_advisor(state: State):
    prompt = f"""
    You are a helpfull senior MARKET ANALYST that gets an idea as an input. You need to Evaluate the market potential, competition, target demographics, and trends:
    Conduct market sizing and competitor research
    Identify target customers and segments
    Assess timing, trends, and macroeconomic influences
    Idea:
    {state['messages']}
    """
    report = llm.invoke([SystemMessage(content=prompt)])
    return {"advisor_reports": {"Market Analyst": report.content}}
Step 9 
def legal_advisor(state: State):
    prompt = f"""
    You are a helpfull Legal Advisor that gets an idea as an input. You need to:
    Identify IP, licensing, and trademark needs
    Spot compliance issues (e.g., GDPR, financial regulations)
    Evaluate contract and partnership considerations
    Idea:
    {state['messages']}
    """
    report = llm.invoke([SystemMessage(content=prompt)])
    return {"advisor_reports": {"Legal Advisor": report.content}}
Step 10 
def technical_advisor(state: State):
    prompt = f"""
    You are a helpfull  Technical/Product Feasibility Expert that gets an idea as an input. You need to:
    Estimate development complexity and time
    Recommend tech stacks or platforms
    Evaluate risk in terms of infrastructure, scalability, and cost
    Idea:
    {state['messages']}
    """
    report = llm.invoke([SystemMessage(content=prompt)])
    return {"advisor_reports": {"Technical Advisor": report.content}}
Step 11 
def strategist_advisor(state: State):
    prompt = f"""
    You are a helpfull Strategist Advisor Expert that gets an idea as an input. You need to:
    Define launch milestones
    Select distribution channels and positioning strategies
    Craft early traction tactics (e.g., community, influencers, PR)
    Idea:
    {state['messages']}
    """
    report = llm.invoke([SystemMessage(content=prompt)])
    return {"advisor_reports": {"Strategist Advisor": report.content}}
Step 12 
def collect_and_report(state: State):
    if len(state["advisor_reports"]) < 4:
        return {}
    report_prompt = f"""
    You are a senior consultant. Combine the four advisor notes below into one clear, 
    structured evaluation report for the founder.
    {state['advisor_reports']}
    """
    report = llm.invoke(report_prompt).content
    display(Markdown("### FINAL REPORT\n\n" + report))
    return {"final_report": report}
Step 13 
builder = StateGraph(State)
Step 14 
builder.add_node("decide_node", decide_node)
builder.add_node("ask_user_node", ask_user_node)
builder.add_node("fanout", lambda state: {}) # does nothing - just a hub
builder.add_node("market_analyst_advisor", market_analyst_advisor)
builder.add_node("legal_advisor", legal_advisor)
builder.add_node("technical_advisor", technical_advisor)
builder.add_node("strategist_advisor", strategist_advisor)
builder.add_node("collect_and_report", collect_and_report)
Step 15 
builder.set_entry_point("decide_node")
builder.add_edge("ask_user_node", "decide_node")
builder.add_conditional_edges(
    "decide_node", route, {"ask_user_node": "ask_user_node", "fanout": "fanout"}
)
builder.add_edge("fanout", "market_analyst_advisor")
builder.add_edge("fanout", "legal_advisor")
builder.add_edge("fanout", "technical_advisor")
builder.add_edge("fanout", "strategist_advisor")

builder.add_edge("market_analyst_advisor", "collect_and_report")
builder.add_edge("legal_advisor", "collect_and_report")
builder.add_edge("technical_advisor", "collect_and_report")
builder.add_edge("strategist_advisor", "collect_and_report")

builder.add_edge("collect_and_report", END)

graph = builder.compile()
Step 16 
display(Image(graph.get_graph(xray=1).draw_mermaid_png()))

Lesson 215: Finalizing the project

00:04.040 --> 00:10.240 We've built all the pieces of our business idea evaluator, the clarification loop, the advisors, 00:10.240 --> 00:12.840 the collection node and the graph wiring. 00:13.200 --> 00:16.360 Now it's time to run the project and see it in action.

Core Concept

Welcome to the final lecture for this section. We've built all the pieces of our business idea evaluator, the clarification loop, the advisors, the collection node and the graph wiring. Now it's time to run the project and see it in action.

Key Points

  • We begin with a simple print statement to greet the user and ask for their business idea.
  • Right after that, we use Python's input function to capture the response.
  • This becomes the very first piece of information our system will use.
  • We save the raw idea string under idea and also add it as the first message in messages.
  • So the conversation starts with the founders input.
  • Then we initialize advisor reports and final report as empty.
  • These will be filled later when the advisors run and the final report is ready.
  • The invoke call passes in the state and the config line sets a thread id.
💡 From the Lecture
01:11.480 --> 01:14.670 Let's say I have an idea about bamboo toothbrushes.
